articles.title: Centre’s Siang dam push turning region into India-China flashpoint
articles.summary: Adi groups oppose Arunachal’s 11,200 MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project, alleging 80% local resistance, rights violations, and rising India-China tensions.
articles.body: PASIGHAT: Adi organisations have alleged that the Centre’s push for the 11,200 MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP) has turned the Siang region into a battleground in the strategic contest between India and China.They have vowed to resist the proposed dam, accusing the govt of overriding local opposition to the project.Adi Bane Kebang-United, one of the leading organisations spearheading the anti-dam movement in Arunachal Pradesh, alleged that nearly 80% of families in the affected villages opposed the project, warning the Centre and the state govt against proceeding with the proposed pre-feasibility study without the consent of local communities.Questioning the project’s strategic rationale, Datik Ratan, spokesperson for the organisation, argued, “Constructing an 11,200 MW dam on the Indian side would not necessarily mitigate the potential impact of a reported 60,000 MW dam on the Chinese side of the border. In our own country, they should not have created a scene as if the British had invaded our areas in the 19th century.”The proposed study involves drilling along the Siang river across Siang, Upper Siang and East Siang districts. While some families have reportedly agreed to the study, the organisation claimed that opposition to the project remained overwhelming, with about 27 Adi-inhabited settlements facing the threat of displacement and submergence.“The govt is pushing ahead despite opposition from 80% of families in the affected villages. This is an assault on tribal rights and an encroachment on our ancestral lands. The govt is responsible for creating disturbances,” Ratan alleged.The organisation further accused the state govt of misleading the Centre to facilitate the survey and alleged that attempts were being made to silence dissent, including by blocking social media accounts of people opposing the project.Claiming that two of his Facebook accounts had been blocked, Ratan challenged chief minister Pema Khandu and the state govt to hold an open debate on the project, saying the protesters were ready to present their arguments with the help of experts.“We are ready to debate with the central govt. articles.title: Mumbai locals hit by double disruption: 3 killed on tracks, 80 services cancelled, delays up to 90 minutes
articles.summary: Central Railway Mumbai disrupted after Kanjurmarg signalling hut fire: 80 locals cancelled, 70–90 min delays, long-distance trains hit; 3 deaths reported.
articles.body: MUMBAI: Three people died in separate incidents on Central Railway tracks on Monday as services went haywire following a signalling hut fire and another disruption, forcing the cancellation of 80 local trains and delaying services by 70-90 minutes.The disruption affected thousands of commuters, stranded passengers in stationary trains for up to 90 minutes and also hit long-distance train operations.Thousands of commuters were stranded in stationary trains for up to 90 minutes, while some walked along the tracks as services operated intermittently on adjoining lines.A 21-year-old Mulund resident, Sahil Thite, died after being hit by a local train while crossing the tracks at Bhandup station. Two people were found dead on tracks between Ghatkopar and Vikhroli stations Monday evening.Police were yet to confirm the cause of their deaths.The CR disruption hit internal semester exams at a few colleges. As students struggled to reach on time, colleges rescheduled the exams.Commuters scrambled to find alternatives to reach their destinations by autorickshaws, buses and Metro on the first day of the week.“A signalling failure occurred at 9.33am after a fire broke out in the signalling hut at Kanjurmarg. Around 24 signals went blank across all six lines between Vikhroli and Bhandup,” said CR’s chief public relations officer Swapnil Nila.This came after a wire of unknown origin was found hanging from the overhead equipment on the Down slow line between Mulund and Thane at 9.23am.The breakdown affected both Main and Harbour lines. The latter also faced a shortage of train crews because personnel and resources were caught up in Main line operations.First, railway officials imposed a power block at 10am following the wire snag and restored the section at 10.48am. But by then, delays had already begun accumulating on the Main Line.Then, as signalling was unavailable following a fire, railway personnel introduced alternative operating procedures, including A-board authority and absolute block working on affected sections.Trains were allowed to proceed only after the prescribed safety clearances, reducing the frequency of movements and causing delays to accumulate across the network.The impact extended beyond suburban services, with both arrivals and departures of long-distance trains delayed as operational restrictions and cascading delays affected train movements, leading to packed platforms across stations.While all the signals were restored by 7.35pm, services continued to be delayed till late night.“An inquiry will be conducted to identify the cause of fire,” said Nila.Kurla GRP has registered a case of accidental death in the Bhandup fatality case.Police said Thite alighted from a train on platform 4, jumped onto the tracks and was attempting to reach platform 3 to board another local when a fast train hit him. articles.title: Dia do Servidor Público: veja onde haverá folga | G1
articles.standfirst: Data é ponto facultativo na administração pública federal, mas estados e municípios podem definir o expediente; trabalhadores da iniciativa privada não têm folga automática.
articles.summary: Data é ponto facultativo na administração pública federal, mas estados e municípios podem definir o expediente; trabalhadores da iniciativa privada não têm folga automática.
articles.body:
Dia do Servidor Público é feriado ou ponto facultativo? Veja quem folga — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

Na próxima quarta-feira (28), é celebrado o Dia do Servidor Público. A data não é feriado nacional, mas é considerada ponto facultativo nos órgãos e entidades da administração pública federal direta, autárquica e fundacional, sem prejuízo da continuidade dos serviços essenciais à população.

Isso significa que estados e municípios podem decidir se haverá expediente nas repartições públicas . Em geral, os governos locais também adotam o ponto facultativo, suspendendo o atendimento ao público, mas mantendo os serviços essenciais, como saúde e segurança.

O Ministério da Gestão e da Inovação em Serviços Públicos (MGI) informou que o ponto facultativo referente ao Dia do Servidor Público Federal será transferido para sexta-feira (30). A portaria que oficializa a mudança será publicada no Diário Oficial da União (DOU) nesta terça-feira (27).

O ponto facultativo também pode ser transferido para outra data , como uma segunda ou sexta-feira. Em 2026, 25 estados transferiram a folga para sexta-feira (30), enquanto apenas dois mantiveram a data original, quarta-feira (28).

Em alguns estados, a mudança permitirá que os servidores abrangidos pela medida tenham quatro dias consecutivos de descanso , considerando o fim de semana e o feriado de Finados, na segunda-feira (2). Veja como fica a situação em cada unidade da Federação:

Diferentemente de um feriado, porém, o ponto facultativo não se aplica automaticamente às empresas privadas . Nesses casos, os funcionários trabalham normalmente, salvo se houver previsão de folga em acordo ou convenção coletiva ou se a própria empresa decidir liberá-los.

Segundo Fábio J. Duque Estrada, advogado trabalhista do AC Burlamaqui Advogados, para saber quem tem direito à folga, é preciso considerar o tipo de vínculo de trabalho.

“A resposta depende, antes de tudo, de quem é o trabalhador e de qual regime jurídico rege a sua relação de trabalho”, explica o advogado.

O g1 conversou com o especialista para explicar como funciona o Dia do Servidor Público. Veja as respostas para as principais dúvidas:

O que fazer se o servidor precisar trabalhar?

Trabalhar no dia 28 dá direito a pagamento em dobro?

A folga no Dia do Servidor Público depende do vínculo profissional e das regras aplicáveis a cada órgão ou empresa.

Servidores públicos federais: o dia 28 é ponto facultativo nos órgãos do governo federal. Mesmo assim, serviços essenciais, como saúde e segurança, podem funcionar normalmente.

Servidores estaduais e municipais: a folga depende das decisões de cada governo. Por isso, é importante consultar o calendário oficial do estado ou município.

Empregados públicos contratados pela CLT: seguem as regras do órgão ou da empresa em que trabalham. No caso das estatais, também podem valer normas internas e acordos coletivos.

Trabalhadores terceirizados em órgãos públicos: não têm folga garantida. Mas, se o órgão fechar e o posto de trabalho ficar inativo, a empresa não pode descontar o dia de quem estava à disposição para trabalhar.

Empregados de empresas privadas: trabalham normalmente, a menos que a empresa conceda folga ou exista alguma regra que garanta a dispensa.

O que fazer se o servidor não ganhar folga?

O servidor deve consultar o calendário oficial, o decreto ou a portaria do órgão para verificar se a folga foi concedida ou transferida para outra data.

Caso seja escalado para trabalhar, especialmente em serviços essenciais, deve verificar as regras internas sobre jornada e eventual compensação.

Em caso de dúvida ou suspeita de descumprimento das normas, a orientação é procurar o setor de recursos humanos, o sindicato da categoria ou assistência jurídica.

Como a folga depende de decisão administrativa, a ausência sem autorização pode ser considerada injustificada e resultar em desconto, conforme as regras aplicáveis ao servidor.

Não, como regra geral. O ponto facultativo não equivale a feriado para fins trabalhistas . Por isso, trabalhar nessa data não garante, por si só, remuneração em dobro .

Para os servidores públicos, eventuais direitos dependem do regime jurídico e das normas aplicáveis ao órgão. Na iniciativa privada, o expediente pode ocorrer normalmente, salvo previsão específica em contrato, acordo ou convenção coletiva.

“Como o ponto facultativo é, juridicamente, um dia útil, quem trabalha no dia 28 recebe a remuneração normal, ressalvadas as horas extras e eventuais vantagens previstas em norma coletiva, lei local ou regulamento interno”, afirma Fábio J. Duque Estrada.

Se o trabalhador ultrapassar a jornada normal, poderá ter direito a horas extras, conforme as regras aplicáveis. Se a data coincidir com um feriado municipal instituído por lei, poderão valer as regras de remuneração ou compensação previstas para o trabalho em feriados.

Em novembro, haverá três feriados nacionais. O primeiro será em 2 de novembro , Dia de Finados, que cairá em uma segunda-feira. Para quem não trabalha aos fins de semana, serão três dias consecutivos de descanso.

Depois, em 15 de novembro, será celebrada a Proclamação da República . Como o feriado cairá em um domingo, não haverá possibilidade de emenda para quem já folga nesse dia.

Já o Dia da Consciência Negra, em 20 de novembro, cairá em uma sexta-feira , permitindo três dias consecutivos de descanso para quem não trabalha aos fins de semana.

Desde 2023, a data é feriado nacional. A mudança foi aprovada pelo Congresso e sancionada em dezembro daquele ano pelo presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) .

20 de novembro , Dia da Consciência Negra (sexta-feira)

articles.title: Quem é a nova rainha da Oktoberfest Blumenau 2027  | G1
articles.standfirst: Natural de Blumenau, Letícia Burckhart Lyra, de 21 anos, vai representar a festa em 2027 ao lado das princesas Bianca Krisanski e Maria Eduarda de Castilhos Costa.
articles.summary: Natural de Blumenau, Letícia Burckhart Lyra, de 21 anos, vai representar a festa em 2027 ao lado das princesas Bianca Krisanski e Maria Eduarda de Castilhos Costa.
articles.body:
Letícia Burckhart Lyra, de 21 anos, foi eleita a nova rainha da Oktoberfest Blumenau . A cerimônia de coroação ocorreu no domingo (25), último dia da festa, que reuniu 680.072 pessoas desde 7 de outubro.

👑Além dela, Bianca Krisanski e Maria Eduarda de Castilhos Costa foram escolhidas como primeira e segunda princesas, respectivamente. O trio vai representar a maior festa alemã das Américas na 42ª edição, marcada para ocorrer de 6 a 24 de outubro de 2027.

A nova rainha trabalha como assistente de importação, tem 1,79 metro de altura, cabelos loiros e olhos azuis-escuros.

Ela mora no bairro Velha, um dos mais tradicionais da cidade, e sempre acompanhou a festa.

“Eu sou blumenauense, então eu sempre acompanhei a festa. Eu sou aquela criança que olhava com os olhinhos brilhando para o carro da realeza e, principalmente, os desfiles são a minha atração preferida. Então, desde pequena, eu tive uma conexão com a festa e estar aqui hoje é a grande realização de um sonho”, contou à NSC TV.

Fora do trabalho e dos compromissos com o evento, seu principal hobby é a leitura.

O esporte também ocupa um lugar importante na vida dela, que costuma jogar vôlei nos fins de semana. Ela já passou pelas categorias de base do Bluvolei, de Blumenau. Nos momentos livres, também gosta de estar com a família e os amigos.

Letícia Burckhart Lyra, de 21 anos, é a nova rainha da Oktoberfest — Foto: Redes sociais/Reprodução

A escolha da realeza encerrou os 19 dias da 41ª Oktoberfest Blumenau. A disputa começou com 21 candidatas, e dez chegaram à final.

Durante a preparação, as concorrentes passaram por avaliações, entrevistas com jurados, testes de vídeo, aulas de oratória e ensaios de coreografia e de passarela.

Nesta segunda-feira (26), Letícia contou que ainda tenta assimilar a conquista e compreender a nova rotina.

“A ficha, na verdade, ainda está caindo. É um misto de emoções muito grande. Aos poucos, a gente começou a rotina hoje e já vai entendendo como vão ser os próximos dias”, afirmou.

Bianca Krisanski, Letícia Burckhart Lyra e Maria Eduarda de Castilhos Costa — Foto: Marcelo Martins, divulgação

articles.title: Wales first minister : ‘We’re within a union that is not a union of equals’
articles.summary: Rhun ap Iorwerth says his country’s relationship with the United Kingdom is unequal and needs to change.
articles.body:
The first minister of Wales says his nation deserves a new deal from the United Kingdom. Rhun ap Iorwerth says its relationship with the UK is not working because the union is not one of equals. That is why he is pushing for an agreement that will fix what he calls “historic unfairness”.

In a letter to the British prime minister, the Welsh first minister has formally requested the transfer of more power to Wales to allow it to control its policing, justice system, rail network and natural resources. His centre-left Welsh nationalist party, Plaid Cymru, came to power in May, ending more than a century of Labour Party dominance in Wales. Just four months into his term, he signed a pact with Scotland and Northern Ireland declaring their right to self-determination, and warning the British Parliament that its time is coming to an end.

He insists that the agreement is not meant to tear down the UK but rather to allow the Welsh government to decide its own future. He says Wales is on the journey towards independence. But he will not push for a referendum this parliament.

articles.summary: Mesmo com a pequena diferença de votos entre Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro no resultado geral, o cenário foi bem diferente em algumas localidades do exterior.
articles.body:
Lula na avenida Paulista. — Foto: Reprodução/X

Neste domingo (25), brasileiros espalhados pelo mundo foram às urnas para decidir quem ocupará o Palácio do Planalto pelos próximos quatro anos. O resultado foi uma vitória apertada de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), com 51,79% dos votos, contra 48,21% de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) . Apesar da disputa acirrada, houveram alguns países onde o petista liderou com folga.

Um deles foi a Palestina, território marcado por um conflito de décadas com Israel e cuja causa é defendida por parte do eleitorado de Lula. Entre os brasileiros que votaram no território palestino, o petista recebeu 1.000 votos, contra apenas 46 de Flávio — o equivalente a 95,60% e 4,40% dos votos válidos, respectivamente.

No primeiro turno o atual presidente também venceu com ampla vantagem por lá, com 93,17% dos votos.

Outro país onde Lula conquistou uma vitória expressiva foi Cuba . Na ilha caribenha, o petista recebeu 43 votos, contra apenas um de Flávio Bolsonaro, o equivalente a 97,73% e 2,27% dos votos válidos, respectivamente.

A vantagem do petista já havia sido esmagadora no primeiro turno, quando Lula obteve 94,75% dos votos, contra 2,63% de Flávio.

Veja como foi as eleição presidencial no exterior — Foto: Bruna Azevedo/Arte g1

Ao todo, 90 países registraram votos no 2º turno das eleições presidenciais brasileiras e Lula o mais votado em 62, enquanto Flávio liderou em 38. Na comparação com o primeiro turno, o candidato do PL virou o resultado em três países e três cidades, enquanto o petista passou à frente em dois países e sete cidades.

A votação no exterior foi organizada em 186 cidades de 134 países e territórios, incluindo a Guiana Francesa.

Mais de 916 mil brasileiros estavam aptos a votar no exterior, mas apenas 381.443 compareceram às urnas.

Segundo o Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), a abstenção foi de 58,37%. Apesar do índice, cerca de 40 mil eleitores a mais votaram no segundo turno em comparação com o primeiro.

Ao todo, 9.762 eleitores votaram nulo ou em branco.

Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) : 171.497 (46,14%)

Na comparação com o segundo turno de 2022, Lula recebeu 47.249 votos a mais no exterior. Na disputa contra Jair Bolsonaro (PL), o petista havia obtido 152.905 votos (51,28%), contra 145.264 (48,72%) do então presidente.

articles.title: Bolsonaro’s party accepts Brazil election after Trump calls vote ‘rigged’
articles.summary: Trump pushes unsubstantiated claims about Brazil’s presidential vote but says he ‘didn’t take sides’ in the race.
articles.body:
The political party of Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has acknowledged the result of Brazil’s presidential run-off, despite the right-wing candidate pledging to annul the outcome.

On Monday, Valdemar Costa Neto, the leader of the right-wing Liberal Party, issued a statement saying his political group had accepted the outcome of the vote.

Still, he echoed Bolsonaro’s concerns about the circumstances surrounding the election.

“We recognise the presidential election results,” Costa Neto said. “But we believe the issues raised need to be properly clarified.”

On Sunday, Bolsonaro was defeated by left-wing incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva by a margin of more than 4.4 million votes.

Bolsonaro has yet to formally concede. In a post-election speech, he called the election results “unacceptable”, citing a last-minute extension to voting hours.

“We will take legal action,” he told supporters. “I will request that these elections be annulled.”

In a video posted on social media on Monday, Bolsonaro also announced that federal police asked him to hand over his passports amid speculation that he could leave the country following his loss.

He said that he would comply with the order and had no plans to leave.

He said the decision came from a Supreme Court justice, and was based on a comment by his US-based brother Eduardo Bolsonaro, who told a US podcast two days before the election that “if my brother does not win, I am in favor that he would leave the country.”

Eduardo cited investigations against his brother.

Brazilian police are probing Flavio Bolsonaro over alleged corruption linked to the financing of the biopic “Dark Horse” about his father.

“I never had any intention of leaving the country. I will surrender my passports and defend myself against this travesty,” Flavio Bolsonaro said.

The right-wing candidate also took up the mantle as “leadership of the opposition” in a separate statement.

An extension to Sunday’s vote had been sought by the campaigns of both candidates — but for different reasons.

Bolsonaro’s camp had pointed to inclement weather that impeded some voters from reaching polling stations. Parts of southern Brazil, considered a right-wing stronghold, had experienced heavy rains on Sunday.

Lula’s campaign, meanwhile, pushed for longer voting hours after it accused some cities of limiting public transportation on election day.

The left-wing leader’s allies framed those reductions in service as an attempt at election interference, aimed at preventing Lula’s working-class base from voting.

Media reports indicated that Pablo Souza, a transportation official in the city of Salvador, was arrested on Sunday over the matter.

In response to the petitions, Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin agreed to extend voting by two hours.

Whereas polls across the country had been slated to close at 5pm Brasilia time (20:00 GMT), Zanin’s order allowed those that had not already closed to remain open until 7pm (22:00 GMT).

Following his loss, Bolsonaro cried foul, saying that the justice’s decision had disadvantaged his voters.

He pointed to Zanin’s relationship with Lula as support: Lula had appointed Zanin to the high court in 2023, and Zanin had formerly served as the left-wing politician’s personal lawyer.

“With a simple stroke of a pen, at the request of a former partner, [Zanin] changed the rules of the game mid-match,” Bolsonaro said in his address on Sunday night.

But experts signalled they were sceptical of Bolsonaro’s claims of malfeasance.

An analysis by Pedro Burgos, a professor at the Brazilian educational institute Insper, found that the extension resulted in 35,000 additional votes across the country, less than 0.03 percent of the total.

That amount was far short of Lula’s 4.4 million vote advantage. The incumbent won more than 64.25 million votes, compared with Bolsonaro’s 59.83 million.

Still, some right-wing allies rallied to Bolsonaro’s support. US President Donald Trump, who has clashed with Lula in the past, told reporters that the vote seemed “rigged”.

“Elections have to be indisputable and it looked very bad to me,” Trump said on Monday. “It looked like another rigged election, frankly.”

Still, Trump stopped short of suggesting that he would get involved on behalf of Bolsonaro, saying instead he “did not take sides” in the election.

Bolsonaro’s refusal to accept his loss has raised concerns about whether he will abide by the democratic process or follow in the footsteps of his father, Jair Bolsonaro, who served as Brazil’s president from 2019 to 2023.

After his defeat to Lula in the 2022 election, the ex-president refused to acknowledge the outcome.

Instead, he and his allies sought to overturn the results, including through a legal challenge , and prosecutors accused him of plotting a coup to prevent the legal transfer of power.

Jair Bolsonaro is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence on coup-related charges.

Separately, he was also barred from serving in public office for eight years, after a court found he had misused his public office to spread misinformation about the election.

Flavio Bolsonaro, along with his siblings, has sought to have his father released. The family has denounced the elder Bolsonaro’s trial as a case of political persecution.

Still, it is unclear whether Flavio Bolsonaro will continue with his legal challenge over Sunday’s election.

The Brazilian news outlet Folha de S Paulo reported on Monday that legal advisers and political allies have convinced Bolsonaro to abandon his quest to have his loss annulled, citing the large margin of Lula’s victory and its validation by the Supreme Court and election authorities.

articles.title: Lula's comeback in Brazil dents Trump's ambitions for Latin America
articles.summary: The Trump-Lula relationship may have thawed, but several issues could reignite tensions between the two leaders.
articles.body:
"Brazil will not accept being anyone's backyard," Brazil's left-wing President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva declared in his election victory speech, a message squarely aimed at Washington.

Domestic elections are rarely won on foreign policy, and this one was no different. But Lula's defiance against what he has described as US interference in Brazilian affairs evoked a patriotic spirit that proved an effective campaigning tool.

It also chimed with his wider brand of politics as a former union leader: standing up to powerful figures.

Paradoxically, it seems to have earned him President Donald Trump's respect. "I like Lula, we get along well," Trump said, responding to the result. "I didn't take sides," he added, before calling the election "terrible" and "rigged".

Lula wins fourth term in dramatic Brazil election comeback

If that sounds muddled, it is because the relationship between the two men is not straightforward. Trump did not explicitly endorse Lula's rival Flávio Bolsonaro, who has refused to recognise the result despite the Supreme Electoral Court finding no evidence of irregularities. But Trump was a close ally of Flávio's father, the former President Jair Bolsonaro.

When I spoke to Lula at his residence about a year ago, relations had hit rock bottom. He told me he had "no relationship" with Trump, that they had never spoken, and that he had no intention of picking up the phone. Trump had recently imposed punitive tariffs on Brazil, largely as a political response to Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial, which the US president called a "witch-hunt" .

Rather than tiptoeing around Trump, as some US allies did, Lula fought back – and it paid off.

He made fiery speeches invoking Brazilian sovereignty, attacked US interference in the judicial process, and took to wearing a blue cap reading "Brazil belongs to Brazilians".

He accused the Bolsonaro family, who had lobbied for the tariffs, of being unpatriotic – a blow to a political right that so often claims patriotism as its terrain.

Even some in the agricultural lobby, typically strong Bolsonaro supporters but reliant on US trade, thought Lula had a point.

The US eventually backed down and reduced the tariffs, although they have since risen again.

The two men spoke at the United Nations and later met in the Oval Office, where Trump called the talks "very good" and Lula said he left "very satisfied".

Another indication, perhaps, that Trump likes a strongman.

Fireworks heard after Lula's victory in São Paulo

So why might Trump be unhappy with the result?

Latin America has swung to the right, with Ecuador, Chile, Colombia, Argentina and Peru all electing presidents closely aligned with the Trump administration. Trump has sought to use these allies to establish US dominance in the Western Hemisphere, a strategy he has dubbed the "Donroe Doctrine".

Christopher Sabatini, senior fellow for Latin America at Chatham House, notes that Trump thought Brazil would be the "10th and biggest prize" after Flávio Bolsonaro won the first round.

Brazil is Latin America's largest economy, and the younger Bolsonaro was expected to join Trump's "Shield of Americas" coalition against narco-trafficking.

Brazil also holds the world's second-largest reserves of rare earth minerals after China, and the US had been eyeing preferential access.

The relationship has thawed, but with four more years ahead for Lula, several issues could reignite tensions.

Brazil accused the US earlier this year of trying to cast doubt on its electoral system and denied visas to two state department officials planning to visit.

The US called this "baseless" and revoked the Brazilian ambassador's visa in response.

If Trump keeps calling this result "rigged", further diplomatic fallout is likely.

Lula has also vehemently opposed US military action in the region, from the seizure of Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela to the bombing of alleged drug-trafficking vessels.

He lambasted Washington for designating Brazil's two major gangs as terrorist organisations after lobbying from Flávio Bolsonaro, and warned of attacks on Brazilian sovereignty.

It is a sensitive subject for a political left that remembers the region's brutal 20th Century dictatorships, many backed by the CIA in the name of stopping communism.

Lula's campaign accused Meta of favouring Flávio Bolsonaro.

Meta denied this but admitted moderation issues and technical errors had wrongly removed some posts or limited their reach.

Lula's supporters responded by sharing his messages through a 10-million-strong WhatsApp group to bypass the algorithms.

Separately, the Trump administration is unhappy with Pix, Brazil's instant payment system, which has boosted the economy, but which the US sees as taking business from Visa and Mastercard.

The relationship has exposed political divisions.

In the campaign, Bolsonaro supporters waved US flags at their rallies and, in one case, an inflatable saying "Trump Nuke Brazil", while Lula and his supporters accused Flávio Bolsonaro of protecting US interests over Brazil's.

The US remains Brazil's second-biggest trading partner after China, and for now the two leaders get on.

Whether that lasts will depend on how far the US tries to intervene in Brazilian affairs, and how bullish Lula is in response.

Who is Lula? From ex-worker and prisoner to Brazil's president again

articles.title: Raskin says oil companies will face consequences for importing Russian diesel
articles.summary: Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), the ranking member on the House Judiciary Committee, said that oil companies will face repercussions if they import Russian diesel, comments that come shortly after President Trump announced a diesel deal with Moscow. In a Monday letter addressed to energy companies, Raskin said oil companies are going to “be held accountable”…
articles.body:
Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), the ranking member on the House Judiciary Committee, said that oil companies will face repercussions if they import Russian diesel, comments that come shortly after President Trump announced a diesel deal with Moscow .

In a Monday letter addressed to energy companies, Raskin said oil companies are going to “be held accountable” in the case that they import barrels of Russian diesel as part of the diesel deal, according to a report from Politico .

The letter was sent to the American Petroleum Institute and American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers, two industry trade groups, per Politico.

“Your members are now on notice that taking part in any effort to help President Putin hawk Russian diesel in the U.S. is a clear and dangerous violation of federal law,” Raskin’s letter reads, Politico reported.

“Those who choose to act in this way proceed at their own risk and will undoubtedly be held accountable to the fullest extent of the law, whether in this Administration — or the next,” he added.

Democrats are expected to win the House in the midterm elections next week, with Decision Desk HQ saying there is a 77 percent chance they will take back the upper chamber. If Democrats pull that off, Raskin could head the House Judiciary Committee.

Trump announced earlier this month that Russia would provide the U.S. and global market with diesel. The move comes only a few weeks out from the midterm elections, in which increasing energy prices are a central issue.

The president said that Moscow would “immediately” give 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and the global marketplace.

“I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter,” he wrote in a post on Truth Social.

The Hill has reached out to the American Petroleum Institute and American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers for comment.

When reached for comment, White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said in a statement that “the Democrats are already telegraphing that, once again, they have no agenda to improve the lives of Americans and will instead continue their decade-long obsession with investigating President Trump.”

articles.title: Stranded hikers cling to steep California mountain ridge as helicopter crew swoops in
articles.summary: Three people trapped on a Northern California cliff were hoisted by helicopter after a Garmin inReach SOS alerted Sierra County authorities.
articles.body: Three people stranded high on a steep Northern California mountainside were rescued by helicopter Sunday after a distress call brought crews racing to their aid. The Sierra County Sheriff’s Office said the group was found on the Sierra Buttes, just south of a lookout tower near the mountain’s summit. Images and video released by officials show the helicopter near the rugged mountainside as rescuers worked to reach the trio. HELICOPTER RESCUE CREW CAUGHT ON CAMERA SAVING 2 CLIMBERS TRAPPED ALONG POPULAR CALIFORNIA BEACH CLIFF The sheriff’s office was alerted around 2:30 p.m. after a Garmin inReach satellite communication device sent an SOS signal to the California Governor’s Office of Emergency Services. Deputies launched a search and rescue response and called in the Nevada County Sheriff’s Search and Rescue Mountain Rescue Team and the Washoe County Sheriff’s Office’s RAVEN helicopter crew. TOURISTS SEEKING 'DRAMATIC' PHOTO ON ISOLATED BEACH TRAPPED BY INCOMING TIDE Once the crew spotted the stranded group, a rescue team member was lowered from the helicopter to reach them. All three were then hoisted off the mountainside and flown to a landing zone, where Sierra County deputies were waiting. "Due to the difficult terrain and hazardous location, a helicopter hoist rescue was necessary," the sheriff’s office said. NORTH CAROLINA CLIMBER AIRLIFTED AFTER PLUNGING 20 FEET DOWN GORGE, SUSTAINING SERIOUS INJURIES The agency thanked the teams involved for their "professionalism, coordination, and assistance" in bringing the rescue to a successful conclusion. The Sierra Buttes rise above the North Yuba River canyon, with a fire lookout near the top of the approximately 8,600-foot mountain, according to the Pacific Crest Trail Association. Authorities did not say how the three people became stranded or whether anyone was injured. The rescue drew praise on social media, where commenters thanked the emergency crews and pointed to the RAVEN helicopter team’s role in helping communities across the region. "To see that Sheriff Balaam uses the RAVEN team to assist anywhere they are needed is outstanding and certainly shows just how valuable the unit has become to the region," one person wrote. Another thanked the rescue teams, writing, "Really awesome work, coordination and knowledge by all involved. Impressive and grateful to have this in our community." "Hats off to our emergency special teams!!" another commenter wrote. "We are all very fortunate that you all do what you do." The dramatic rescue came after two other high-profile rescues on Northern California mountains earlier this month. MISSING 72-YEAR-OLD HIKER FOUND ALIVE DAYS AFTER FRIGHTENING 100-FOOT FALL LEFT HER BADLY INJURED Last week, a 39-year-old Florida man was flown to a hospital after he fell through a snow bridge and severely injured his leg on the Whitney Glacier. Rescuers reached the injured climber the following morning, but bad weather prevented an aerial extraction. Crews ultimately carried him to a viable helicopter landing zone the next day, the Siskiyou County Sheriff’s Office said. Both were uninjured, authorities said.

articles.title: Deported migrant who '60 Minutes' painted as sympathetic family man claimed he was gay on asylum application
articles.summary: Moussa Diawara's 2009 asylum application claimed he was a gay man facing persecution in Mali, appearing to contradict the family man narrative shown on "60 Minutes."
articles.body: Sunday's "60 Minutes" featured the story of a deported Malian national who was painted as a loving husband and father despite insisting he was homosexual on his asylum application. The CBS News segment focused on Moussa Diawara and his family, speaking to his wife, 16-year-old son and 12-year-old daughter. But the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) says Diawara, who arrived in the United States in 2001, is actually an example of widespread fraud throughout the immigration system. "The ‘60 Minutes’ sob story tonight highlighted an illegal alien and his wife and two children. One problem. articles.title: Russia halts strikes on Ukraine’s Kherson as Oleshky ceasefire takes effect
articles.summary: The localised ceasefire, secured by US First Lady Melania Trump, will allow evacuations and aid deliveries to Oleshky.
articles.body:
Russia has suspended strikes on the Ukrainian province of Kherson as a localised ceasefire takes effect ahead of a humanitarian mission led by the United States’ First Lady Melania Trump.

The pause in fighting started at 01:00 GMT on Tuesday, according to the Russian Defence Ministry, to allow for an aid mission into the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Kherson later this week.

The mission will enable aid deliveries and allow evacuations from the front-line town, which is suffering acute shortages of food, medicine and other basic supplies.

The agreement was announced on October ‌23 and brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, with the additional involvement of Pope Leo, as Washington seeks to revive peace talks between Moscow and Kyiv after more than four and a half years of fighting.

Up to 2,000 people remain in Oleshky. They have been unable to leave because of explosive mines and drone attacks in the area, according to the United Nations.

The town, which had a pre-war population of 24,000 people, lies on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River in the partially occupied Kherson region, opposite Kherson city, which is held by Ukrainian forces. Russian troops seized Oleshky during the first ⁠days of their February 2022 invasion and have controlled it ever since.

Oleshky has suffered extensive war damage and was hit hard by flooding after the destruction of the nearby Kakhovka Dam in 2023.

The localised ceasefire is due to last through Saturday, or longer, amid deep mistrust between Russia and Ukraine that has thwarted previous attempts at ceasefires.

Negotiators involved in the aid mission said doctors, medicines, food supplies and water would be taken to Oleshky before evacuation corridors are opened.

articles.title: NAACP decries viral videos of group wearing KKK robes in El Paso, Texas
articles.summary: The videos were posted to social media over the weekend. “It hurts,” said the El Paso branch president of the NAACP.
articles.body: Police and the El Paso, Texas, branch of the NAACP are condemning a group of people, possibly including youths, who were shown wearing Ku Klux Klan-style white robes and hoods in viral social media videos. The videos show the group walking on a neighborhood street, which police indicated is in El Paso. In one video, the person recording can be heard laughing and telling the group, “Y’all gotta yell something, güey.” (“Güey” is Spanish slang, most commonly used in Mexico, akin to “dude” in English.) Carl B. Dwyer Jr., the NAACP’s El Paso branch president, denounced the display at a news conference Monday morning as deeply hurtful to Black Americans, for whom the KKK has been a real-life terror since the Civil War. “Many believe that it’s just a joke,” he said after supporters joined in to sing “Lift Every Voice and Sing,” the hymn often referred to as the Black national anthem. “It hurts,” Dwyer said. “It hurts.” El Paso Police Chief Peter Pacillas said in a statement that the department was looking into whether the group, “reportedly including young people,” violated any laws, including disorderly conduct “or other applicable offenses.” “Symbols and language associated with the Ku Klux Klan represent a history of terror, violence, and racial hatred,” he said. “They have no place in our community. Treating that history as a costume or a joke is unacceptable and contrary to the values of respect and safety that define El Paso.” Artie C. Maxwell Jr., pastor of El Paso’s Mount Zion Baptist Church, also spoke at Monday’s news conference and provided historical context for a city that briefly sympathized with the Confederacy. “We may think that it is a joke, but it’s not a joke when it comes to the lives that have come before us,” he said. “God, that many have died at the hands of those who have worn those costumes.” Pacillas invited those with information about the incident to step forward. “Free expression has limits when it crosses into conduct that threatens public order or the safety of others,” he said. Dwyer urged local educators to remind students of history and its influence on the present. “We’re calling on all of the superintendents, all of the school districts, please, speak up. Please, do something about this,” he said.

articles.title: Britain converted a nearly 200-year-old railway worker's hut into a bat shelter; a winter inspection found a whiskered bat hibernating inside
articles.summary: A disused railway fogging hut beside a tunnel in the Cotswolds countryside, a type of structure dating back almost 200 years, has been converted into a
articles.body: A disused railway fogging hut beside a tunnel in the Cotswolds countryside, a type of structure dating back almost 200 years, has been converted into a dedicated bat shelter after a whiskered bat was found hibernating inside. The conversion turns an overlooked piece of working railway heritage into a hibernaculum, a safe place where bats can spend the winter, and a summer roost as well. National Highways, which looks after the site as part of its historical railways estate, expects the improvements to encourage more bats to settle there in the years ahead, supporting its wider work to protect biodiversity.The whiskered bat found hibernating in a historic railway fogging hutA whiskered bat, a small species found in Britain, was discovered hibernating inside the disused hut during an ecological survey in autumn 2024, according to National Highways. The discovery surprised the team because the hut was in poor condition, with graffiti-covered walls and openings that left it exposed to the elements. Whiskered bats are among Britain's native bat species and use sheltered spaces to roost and hibernate through the colder months. Finding one inside the abandoned railway structure prompted the team to explore how it could be adapted to provide safer, more suitable conditions for bats in winter and summer.How a minor tunnel repair survey uncovered a hibernating bat in a graffiti-covered railway hutIn autumn 2024 a tunnel was due to receive minor repairs, and the ecological survey carried out by partner Jacobs revealed an old, disused hut beside it. The hut was not part of the planned works, but the team checked it anyway. An ecologist working on the site said in comments published by National Highways that the discovery was a surprise, because the structure was in poor condition. Children had clearly been messing about in it, graffiti covered the walls and it was open to the elements, whereas bats usually “prefer somewhere that is more enclosed”.How builders turned an exposed hut into a safe hibernation homeThe tunnel works were completed under a bat licence, and the team decided that a few enhancements could turn the hut into a lasting home for bats. When the construction crew began, they found an old chimney inside, which left a hole in the roof where smoke once escaped. Large roof openings let in air and water, and hibernating bats prefer humidity and a stable low temperature, so the chimney was removed and the top sealed over. The entrance was bricked up, leaving a small post box-style opening near the top. Bats can fly in and out easily, while people and predators cannot disturb them.Clear corrugated sheeting inside the hut for roosting bats and a window for ecologistsInside, the team fitted corrugated sheeting at varying heights, improving the chance that bats find suitable conditions. Some species, known as crevice-dwelling bats, like to crawl behind gaps to roost, and the grooves of the sheeting provide exactly that. Because the material is clear, ecologists can look inside in future to see whether the bats are using their new home and to monitor them. The ecology team will keep checking the hut over the coming months and years, helping to protect Britain’s native species.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Melania Trump-brokered one-city ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine takes effect
articles.summary: A localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the occupied city of Oleshky that First Lady Melania Trump helped to broker has now gone into effect, officials on both sides said Tuesday.
articles.body: A localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the occupied city of Oleshky that First Lady Melania Trump helped to broker has now gone into effect, officials on both sides said Tuesday. Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s parliament commissioner for human rights, said the ceasefire went into effect at 3:00 a.m. Kyiv time Tuesday in a post to X. Russia’s defense ministry said on Telegram it stopped shelling in the direction of Oleshky at the same time Tuesday. The pause in fighting is intended to help evacuate elderly residents and bring urgently needed humanitarian aid to the town on the frontlines of the fighting, which has been occupied by Russia since the first days of the invasion in 2022. Ukrainian authorities have said about 1,700 people remain in Oleshky. Lubinets said the ceasefire is “part of a humanitarian mission being carried out with the mediation and coordination of US First Lady Melania Trump, in cooperation with Yana Lantratova, Russia’s Commissioner for Human Rights.” It was unclear how long the ceasefire was due to last. Elsewhere, fighting continued. A 46-year-old woman was killed and more than a dozen people were injured in an attack on Kyiv, which also damaged a bridge, Ukraine’s Emergency Service said. Russia’s military said it carried out a “massive strike” targeting Ukrainian military facilities, a logistics center in Kharkiv, and transport infrastructure in Kyiv. It also said it intercepted and destroyed 222 Ukrainian drones over its territory. The first lady announced Friday she had worked with Ukrainian and Russian leadership to secure the localized ceasefire as the “exclusive intermediary.” “The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks,” Melania Trump said in a statement Friday. “Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require,” she added. “Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine.” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Saturday Kyiv had been working to negotiate this deal for “some time.” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov credited Trump for her “significant contribution.” Donald Trump praised his wife’s efforts on Friday, saying “they contacted both sides, and both sides wanted to do it.” He said that her focus remains on helping the children impacted by the war. Pope Leo also discussed the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky on an October 16 phone call with Putin while in the hospital recovering from lung cancer surgery, according to the Vatican. The first lady’s office said last week that the circumstances of Oleshky came to her attention during a private discussion at the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York in September.

articles.title: Australian judge rejects prisoner’s human rights challenge to Vegemite ban
articles.summary: Andre McKechnie had argued in court that withholding the polarizing yeast-based spread breached his human right to “enjoy his culture as an Australian.”
articles.body: MELBOURNE, Australia — A prisoner lost his challenge Monday to an Australian state’s ban on inmates eating Vegemite after he argued in court that withholding the polarizing yeast-based spread breached his human right to “enjoy his culture as an Australian.” Andre McKechnie, 55, who is serving a life sentence for murder, took his battle for the salty, sticky, black-brown byproduct of brewing beer to the Supreme Court of the state of Victoria last year. He had argued that being refused Vegemite denied him his right under the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act to “enjoy his culture as an Australian in the community with other persons of Australian background,” court documents showed. Justice Claire Harris accepted that prison authorities’ refusal to allow McKechnie Vegemite “limited his cultural rights” under the charter. But she found that the ban was justified in meeting authorities’ goals of removing illicit drugs and alcohol from the prison system. “The limitation on Mr. McKechnie’s ability to enjoy Vegemite in community with other persons of Australian background is primarily that he is a prisoner,” Harris wrote in her 47-page judgment. Prison officials testified at a trial in July that Vegemite had been banned throughout the state’s 12 prisons for the past 20 years because it could potentially impair sniffer dogs’ ability to detect narcotics and could be used to brew alcohol because of its yeast content. McKechnie, who represented himself in court by video link from maximum-security Barwon Prison west of Melbourne, argued that the fact that neighboring New South Wales state did not ban Vegemite from its prisons was evidence that there were “less restrictive means reasonably available” to achieve such drug and alcohol outcomes. Most Australians revere Vegemite as an unfairly maligned culinary icon, and more than 80% of Australian households are estimated to have a jar in their pantries. Vegemite is typically considered an acquired taste at best by those who weren’t raised on it. The last U.S. president to visit Australia, Barack Obama, once said: “It’s horrible.” McKechnie had initially testified that the lack of Vegemite had contributed to his thiamine deficiency. He said both Vegemite and pork were sources of thiamine, also known as vitamin B1. As a Jew who observed kosher law, he told the court he couldn’t eat pork either and took daily doses of the vitamin. Vegemite has long been marketed as a source of B vitamins thiamine (B1), riboflavin (B2), niacin (B3) and folate (B9), which are promoted as healthy additions to the diets of growing children. But McKechnie dropped the thiamine issue as “not important” after lawyers for the prison authorities objected to his evidence. McKechnie said not eating Vegemite made him feel “deprived of being able to practice my Australian culture, sad and disconnected from my family and community.” The judge responded that “it is difficult to accept that the inability to consume Vegemite, rather than the fact of his imprisonment, is a material cause of his sadness and disconnection from his family and community.” McKechnie cited an article published in the food studies journal Gastronomica in 2003 that said, “Vegemite may be the best predictor of national identity of any food in the world.” The article, based on research by Australia’s Queensland University in 1995, found that a “taste for the spread strongly correlates with early exposure and to Australian birth and ancestry.” McKechnie also referred to the Australian Olympic Committee overturning a Chinese import ban on Vegemite ahead of the 2008 Summer Olympics in Beijing. He cited Australian band Men at Work’s 1980s international hit “Down Under” that mentions a “Vegemite sandwich.” On the effectiveness of smearing contraband with Vegemite, McKechnie cited a Melbourne newspaper article from 2017 that reported a man’s unsuccessful attempt to use the odor of the spread to conceal illicit drugs that he attempted to smuggle into a music festival in Victoria. The attempt was thwarted by police sniffer dogs. The judge upheld prison authorities’ argument that McKechnie had failed to provide any proper foundations for his opinion that Vegemite does not interfere with drug sniffer dogs. McKechnie also argued that Vegemite contained “no live yeast” and that any piece of fruit would be more useful in making alcohol than the spread. A state prison department manager, Kevin White, cited publicly available research that said Vegemite helped home-brewed beer ferment more quickly. Vegemite’s owner, Bega Group, did not respond to a request for comment Monday.

articles.title: North Carolina judge backs developer’s 750MW data centre project after county paused new facilities over concerns about water, power and pollution
articles.summary: A North Carolina judge has ruled in favour of a developer challenging Chatham County’s 12-month moratorium on data centre development, in a case involving
articles.body: A North Carolina judge has ruled in favour of a developer challenging Chatham County’s 12-month moratorium on data centre development, in a case involving a proposed 750-megawatt facility that is also expected to include cryptocurrency mining. Chatham Journal reported that County Attorney Emily Meeker said the ruling meant the project could proceed without being subject to the new regulations. The court order, signed by Superior Court Judge John M. Morris on 17 September 2026, granted summary judgment to Eco TIP West LLC on liability and attorneys’ fees. It did not determine the amount of damages, which remain for further proceedings. The decision follows a temporary moratorium adopted in February covering data centre development in unincorporated areas of Chatham County, as officials studied the potential effects of large facilities on infrastructure and natural resources.County approved moratorium in FebruaryThe Chatham County Board of Commissioners adopted the temporary moratorium on 11 February 2026. Eco TIP’s complaint and press reports described the commissioners’ 11 February vote as unanimous. The ordinance covers data centres, data processing facilities, cryptocurrency mining operations and associated uses in unincorporated areas of the county. The county said the pause would give officials time to study the effects of these uses and develop zoning rules. Its published concerns include infrastructure capacity, water use, energy demand, noise, air pollution and water pollution. In its 12 February announcement, the county said it would study how other communities regulate these uses and develop zoning rules to mitigate negative impacts. The moratorium was set to last 12 months, ending on 11 February 2027, or earlier if new zoning regulations were adopted.Eco TIP’s proposed facility is planned for Triangle Innovation Point West, an industrial site near Moncure. The company’s complaint describes a project with a capacity of approximately 750 megawatts that would include cryptocurrency mining. Eco TIP says it has spent more than $11 million developing the project. The company’s court brief also says at least 30 local governments in North Carolina have adopted similar moratoria. The case may be the first court challenge to a data centre moratorium in the state, according to reporting by The News & Observer republished by Yahoo.Developer and county disputed the project’s statusEco TIP filed its lawsuit in April 2026, arguing that the moratorium could not lawfully be applied to its project. The complaint challenged the moratorium under North Carolina’s planning and development laws and state constitution, and asserted a federal substantive due process claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1983. It also raised claims concerning down-zoning, statutory exemptions, vested rights and permit-choice rights. Eco TIP requested a jury trial and damages exceeding $25,000. Eco TIP also alleged, “upon information and belief”, that county officials met behind closed doors with opponents of data centres generally before 20 January 2026. This is an allegation in the complaint, not a judicial finding. That allegation is part of the company’s case and should not be treated as a judicial finding.The county disputed the developer’s account. In its response opposing summary judgment, it argued that a zoning interpretation letter confirming data centres were a permitted use in the relevant industrial district did not amount to approval to build. The county also contended that Eco TIP’s application was incomplete when the moratorium took effect, citing outstanding requirements, including Appearance Commission approval and a fee. It disputed the company’s claim that its spending demonstrated qualifying reliance on prior county action and argued that further discovery was necessary. These were competing positions in the lawsuit. The judge’s short order does not identify which of Eco TIP’s legal arguments was decisive.Court leaves damages unresolvedJudge Morris heard the summary-judgment motion on 31 August and signed the order on 17 September. The order, filed the following day, states that there was no genuine issue of material fact and that Eco TIP was entitled to judgment as a matter of law. It grants the company’s motion as to liability and attorneys’ fees. The company was directed to file an itemised affidavit of its attorneys’ fees and costs within 14 days of the order’s entry. The court reserved the determination and award of damages for later proceedings and directed the parties to confer and submit a proposed scheduling order for resolving those claims within 21 days. The order does not set a damages amount or provide a detailed explanation of the legal reasoning behind the result. Nor does it declare every data centre moratorium in North Carolina invalid. The ruling concerns Eco TIP’s challenge to Chatham County’s action and the claims in this particular case.County meetings continue after rulingAfter the decision, County Attorney Emily Meeker said the county had adopted the moratorium to pause data centre construction while it developed zoning regulations for intensive land uses. She expressed disappointment with the ruling and said the county was considering its legal options, according to Chatham Journal reporting published on 29 September.The Board of Commissioners held or scheduled closed sessions concerning the handling or possible settlement of Eco TIP West LLC v. Chatham County after the ruling. The outcome of those discussions could not be independently established from the records verified for this article. The court’s order leaves the amount of damages and attorneys’ fees unresolved. The subsequent legal proceedings will determine those outstanding issues.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Israel heads to the polls as shift to the right dominates critical election
articles.summary: Netanyahu seeks to extend rule at helm of far right alliance facing off against predominantly right-wing bloc.
articles.body:
Israel is heading to the polls on Tuesday in a closely contested election that is being described as one of the most important in its history.

The vote is the first since the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023 and the subsequent genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza, as well as a wider conflict that has seen Israel carry out attacks on Iran, Lebanon, Yemen, Syria and Qatar.

Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, is seeking to extend his tenure after leading the country’s most right-wing governing coalition which brought together far-right ultranationalists and ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties.

Wanted by the International Criminal Court on charges of war crimes in Gaza and faced with a long-running corruption trial, he is fighting for his political survival against a self-styled Zionist opposition bloc that has fundamentally embraced a right-wing approach to Israel’s challenges. Questions over accountability for alleged security failures , disputes over ultra-Orthodox military service and efforts to exclude Arab-led parties dominated the campaign.

This has further dampened already low expectations that the vote would offer any meaningful improvement to the lives of Palestinians, as deadly attacks continue almost daily in Gaza despite a yearlong “ceasefire”, while settler pogroms and Israeli army raids have intensified in the occupied West Bank.

“The entire Israeli political system operates within the racist framework of Jewish supremacy,” Yehouda Shenhav-Shahrabani, a noted Israeli sociologist, told Al Jazeera.

“None of the leaders who present themselves as an alternative to Netanyahu can genuinely be described as left-wing. The horrifying reality we are witnessing is not simply the product of Netanyahu or the far right. It is rooted in Zionist political thought itself, which is structured around the principle of Jewish supremacy. There is no way around this fundamental fact,” he said.

Israel’s shift to the right did not begin with the establishment of Netanyahu’s most recent government in 2022, or what polls show to have been the rightward lurch that took place across Israel following the Hamas-led attack of 2023. Rather, the collapse of the peace process with the Palestinians and repeated security crises over the past few decades have combined to systematically erode the political centre and left, giving rise to landmark legislative milestones such as the 2018 Nation-State Law , which formally enshrined Jewish supremacy and the continued and violent expansion of illegal Israeli settlements into occupied Palestinian territory with little or no government restraint.

However, if the drift to the right was there beforehand, most analysts agree that its speed has accelerated to unprecedented heights under the latest Netanyahu government, which faced accusations of seeking to reshape the country in its own image.

They point to attempts to strip the Supreme Court of its power to review government actions and the flouting of its rulings on conscripting the ultra-Orthodox minority whose political support helped sustain the governing coalition, as well as the presence of figures such as far-right provocateur and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and religious Zionist Bezalel Smotrich , Israel’s finance minister.

Together, in return for their seat at the table, both ministers offered crucial support to the controversial judicial overhaul that Netanyahu – himself on trial for bribery, fraud and breach of trust, charges he denies – launched in the early months of 2023 and which continues to this day. Similarly, both ministers have provided encouragement and cover for the surge in violence across the West Bank, while deflecting attempts to hold the coalition accountable for the alleged security failures that preceded the Hamas-led attack.

“If Netanyahu loses the election and, say, [Gadi] Eisenkot becomes the new prime minister, the main initial change will be the atmosphere, the vibe, as Netanyahu stirs deep emotions domestically,” Ahron Bregman, an Israeli analyst and senior teaching fellow at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.

“Those who admire him, and there are many in Israel, regard him as God. Those who hate him, and there are many in Israel, hate him deeply,” said Bregman. “He’s a very divisive figure. A new prime minister is likely to calm things down.”

With the vote closely watched across the region and beyond, analysts also say the stakes go beyond the names on the ballot and cut through to the very nature of the character and future of Israel.

“The decision facing Israel of whether to retain a Netanyahu-led government or not is ultimately the decision on whether to live in a functioning democracy or a democracy in name only,” Yossi Mekelberg, a senior fellow at Chatham House, told Al Jazeera.

“It’s the choice between maintaining the occupation of the West Bank or annexing it entirely and the population’s ‘voluntary migration’ from there, as figures within the government have actually suggested.”

A respect for process and the rule of law would likely return to government in the event of an opposition win, added Bregman, a sharp contrast with what he described as Netanyahu’s approach to government. However, to expect too great a change in the overall direction of policy would be to miss the point.

“Don’t be mistaken,” he cautioned. “Israel, particularly after 7 October, turned sharply to the right, and any new government will reflect and mirror this reality.”

What will not be on the ballot, analysts and observers say, is any opportunity to challenge a foreign and security policy that has underpinned the killing of more than 74,000 people in Gaza, the increased violence across the West Bank and the launching of multiple wars, including one on Iran that has seen key energy routes choked and has left global markets reeling.

None of the mainstream candidates for office in October have talked about including Arab-led parties in any potential coalition. In Israel’s popular media, references to the leaders of Ra’am or the Joint List are typically used by rival candidates to denounce each other for considering a future coalition with Palestinian politicians, now or in the past.

Shenhav-Shahrabani, the sociologist, said the ultra-Orthodox parties would still be welcome in government after the vote by either coalition, while the Arab-led parties representing the Palestinian citizens of Israel – one-fifth of the total population – would be excluded by a system built upon prejudice.

“The distinction is not between democratic and anti-democratic forces, but between Jews and Palestinians. As long as there is no genuine binational political vision, racism and the systematic restriction of Palestinian rights will remain fundamental features of Israeli society,” he said.

If that framework shapes who is allowed into government, it also shapes what the campaign is about. Netanyahu’s challengers largely framed their disagreements with him as questions of competence, timing and accountability for the alleged failures that preceded October 7, rather than challenges to the way Palestinians are treated.

For critics, that omission is not an oversight but a reflection of where the Israeli mainstream now sits: among the issues at stake in the election, none amounted to a referendum on the genocide in Gaza. “How can it be a referendum on genocide, or anything to do with the treatment of Palestinians in Gaza?” asked Daniel Levy, a former Israeli government adviser.

“You would have to have one side arguing it was a good thing and the other arguing it was a bad thing, let alone acknowledging that it was a genocide. So, no, obviously none of that is on the ballot,” he said.

“The treatment of Palestinians by the Israeli state and military is a consensus among Zionist parties,” added Levy, with differences among them primarily resting on “whether it’s the state’s job to oppress Palestinians, or if the settler militias also have a role – a significant role – to play”.

articles.title: Tracking the money: The biggest donors in the 2026 US midterm elections
articles.summary: The 50 biggest contributors have poured $2.77bn into the race, led by Elon Musk’s $446m for Republican-aligned groups.
articles.body:
The 2026 US midterms are on track to be the most expensive in the country’s history. Spending on political advertising alone is projected to reach $11.6bn, more than in any previous election cycle, including the 2024 presidential race, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact.

Much of that money comes from wealthy donors, political nonprofits and businesses seeking to shape Washington’s priorities, and some of it passes through networks of organisations before it is spent.

In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera uses Federal Election Commission data to trace the billionaires, financiers and companies behind the largest contributions ahead of the November 3 vote .

The 50 largest donors contributed $2.77bn

The 50 largest donors and organisations have so far contributed a combined $2.77bn during the 2026 midterm election cycle.

Republican-aligned contributors accounted for $1.67bn, or about 60 percent of donations, double the $832m (30 percent) from Democratic-aligned contributors.

The remaining $264m, about 10 percent, came from contributors classified as bipartisan or special interest, including groups backing sports betting and cryptocurrency.

Individuals can donate up to $3,500 per election to a US federal candidate’s campaign in the 2025–26 election cycle. Yet some of the people on this list have given hundreds of millions of dollars.

That is legal because most of the money went not to candidates but to super political action committees, or super PACs, which can accept donations of any size.

A super PAC is a group that can raise and spend unlimited sums to support or oppose candidates, mainly through advertising. The main condition is that it must not coordinate its spending with candidates or their campaigns.

They emerged in 2010 after two court rulings paved the way for unlimited spending on elections by groups independent of candidates.

Super PACs must report their donors to the Federal Election Commission (FEC), the US agency that oversees federal elections. But some major contributors, including One Nation and Majority Forward, are nonprofit groups that do not have to disclose their own donors.

This can hide where political money originally comes from, a practice known as “dark money”.

But Lawrence Lessig, a professor of law and leadership at Harvard Law School and a campaign finance reform advocate, argues that the money is hidden only from voters.

“It’s not dark to the politicians. It’s dark to us,” he told Josh Rushing on Al Jazeera’s Let’s Focus , in a debate on money in US elections with Bradley Smith, a former chairman of the Federal Election Commission. “Nobody’s confused from the politician’s side about where this money is coming from, and they know what they need to do.”

Elon Musk, the world’s richest man and head of Tesla and SpaceX, is the largest individual contributor of the cycle, with $446m, according to Federal Election Commission data.

He is followed by Elizabeth and Richard Uihlein, founders of the shipping supplies company Uline, and Jeff and Janine Yass. Jeff Yass cofounded the trading firm Susquehanna International Group.

All three have given to Republican-aligned groups.

Elizabeth and Richard Uihlein: $150 million

The largest Democratic-aligned donors are George Soros, the billionaire investor and founder of the Open Society Foundations; Mike Bloomberg, the former New York City mayor and founder of the financial data company Bloomberg; and LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman and his wife, Michelle Yee.

Reid Hoffman and Michelle Yee: $41 million

Four individual donors have each given more than $100m. For Lessig, that concentration, not the overall cost of elections, is the real concern.

“The problem isn’t the spending. The problem is the concentration of donors,” he said. “If you don’t have $100 million to put on the table, you’re not going to matter in the way that we think that people ought to matter in a democracy.”

Which organisations contributed the most?

Political nonprofits led the organisational rankings, alongside cryptocurrency firms and an industrial conglomerate.

On the Republican side, the largest was One Nation, a nonprofit aligned with Senate Republican leadership, followed by American Action Network, which is linked to House Republican leadership. On the Democratic side, Majority Forward and House Majority Forward, nonprofits allied with the party’s Senate and House leadership, led the way.

American Prosperity Alliance: $50.7 million

Economic Opportunity Fund: $41.5 million

Cryptocurrency companies also featured prominently. Coinbase, the largest US crypto exchange, gave $57.8m, followed by Ripple, the blockchain payments company, with $49.6m, and Foris DAX, the company behind Crypto.com, with $39m.

The industrial conglomerate Koch gave $46.8m, while the sports betting company DraftKings contributed $40.4m.

articles.title: Israel heads to polls for pivotal election defined by security and democracy
articles.summary: Many fear neither of the leading political blocs will win enough seats for a majority - meaning weeks or months of political wrangling may lie ahead.
articles.body:
Israelis are heading to the polls for what many view as one of the most pivotal elections in the country's history.

Polling published on Friday suggests incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu is in a near neck-and-neck race with former military chief Gadi Eisenkot to become prime minister.

But neither of their political blocs are projected to win the 61 seats needed to form a majority government - meaning weeks or months of political wrangling may lie ahead.

The campaign has been shaped by the issue of security - with the opposition bloc hammering Netanyahu for the unprecedented security failure that led to the 7 October Hamas-led attacks on Israel, in which nearly 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken back to Gaza as hostages.

They have pushed for an independent commission of inquiry into the attacks - something Netanyahu has long resisted, insisting it would be biased against him.

Despite the opposition's attack lines, Netanyahu has once again framed himself as "Mr Security" - pointing to what he says are strategic victories in Israel's wars across the Middle East and his close relationship with US President Donald Trump.

Israel's proportional representation system means governments have always been coalitions - and the race to power can, and has, produced unexpected alliances. But this election looks especially tight - and lines in the sand have already been drawn.

Eisenkot, who leads the newly formed Yashar Party, is the main figure in the so-called "change bloc", a collection of parties who have ideological differences but share the goal of ousting Netanyahu.

Other leaders in the bloc include former prime minister Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman - both right-wingers who take hardline positions on security - and Yair Golan, a left-leaning former general.

For Netanyahu, a titan of Israeli politics who first served as prime minister in 1996, a return to power will hinge on another alliance with the far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties that make up his current governing coalition - the most right-wing in Israel's history .

There are two Arab party blocs in the running too, as about one-fifth of Israel's population is Arab - many of whom describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. In theory, they could prove kingmakers . But all but one of the leading Jewish parties have ruled out working with them.

The opposition bloc also point to what they see as threats to democracy under Netanyahu, who faces an ongoing trial on corruption charges - which he denies - and is still pursuing contentious plans for reforms to the judicial system, which led to mass protests before the 7 October attacks.

On Sunday, Israel's Channel 12 reported that Netanyahu had pushed for last-minute military action that could trigger a confrontation with Iran prior to the elections - but was opposed by his own military chief Eyal Zamir. The following day, CNN reported that he had also tried to persuade Trump to carry out new strikes on Iran, but that Trump had refused to give the green light. Netanyahu denied both reports.

He also made headlines in the final days of his campaign for posting an AI-generated image of a nuclear bomb hitting Tel Aviv, warning that he is the only leader who can protect Israel "if the Iranians acquire nuclear weapons". Eisenkot called him "hysterical".

Another dominating issue has been conscription, with Netanyahu's government failing to enforce a Supreme Court ruling that ultra-Orthodox Jewish men in full-time religious study should be conscripted to the military - a highly divisive move as thousands of others have been conscripted to fight in recent wars.

Eisenkot takes a broadly similar position to Netanyahu on Gaza, and has pledged to end Hamas rule in the territory within 18 months, through a US-led peace plan or, if necessary, military means.

Israel has continued to strike Gaza almost every day since a ceasefire was agreed last year, saying it is targeting Hamas operatives. The Israeli military has killed more than 74,000 people since the start of the war, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

Israel has faced growing international condemnation over its conduct in the war, and relations with its allies around the world have deteriorated.

Eisenkot largely supports Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank - which are illegal under international law - but wants to crack down on extremist Jewish settlers whose attacks are at an all-time high, according to UN figures. He has also spoken about creating the conditions for "autonomy or a state-minus" for Palestinians - under ultimate Israeli security control.

The two-state solution - the creation of an independent Palestinian state in peaceful coexistence alongside Israel - has all but disappeared from mainstream Israeli politics.

Though some have speculated the Arab parties may end up informally propping up an Eisenkot-led minority government - Lieberman, a key prospective member, has ruled out being part of such an arrangement.

Red lines like these mean the electoral arithmetic is complex - but it remains to be seen what kind of concessions, deals and U-turns can be reached once the results come in.

An unprecedented 70,000 people have reportedly flown home from abroad to vote, while half a million are set to cast ballots for the first time.

At 22:00 (20:00 GMT) on Tuesday, Israeli broadcasters will publish exit polls. These will give some indication of the direction of voting, but can vary significantly.

Up and down the country, Israelis will gather to watch the results trickle in, with Netanyahu's Likud meeting in Jerusalem and Eisenkot's Yashar - formed only last year - assembling in Tel Aviv.

Hundreds of thousands of Israeli soldiers and reservists will also cast ballots, but many of those votes will not begin being counted until Wednesday - meaning there may be a late boon for the right-wing parties who are thought to have strong support from that demographic.

Though often framed as a run-off between Eisenkot and Netanyahu, it is possible another leader could take power, if they were to withhold their party's support for a coalition unless given the top job.

An outcome dreaded by many is political deadlock - where no bloc is able to reach a majority, and a minority government cannot be formed. In that scenario, new elections would be called, with Netanyahu to remain as interim prime minister.

Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five separate elections as parties struggled time and again to co-operate.
