articles.title: Zohran Mamdani announces $2 million investment in New York Aquarium renovation; money will support upgrades to Sea Cliffs exhibit housing seals, sea otters and sea lions
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has announced a $2 million investment in the New York Aquarium’s Sea Cliffs Exhibit Renovation Project, bringing
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has announced a $2 million investment in the New York Aquarium’s Sea Cliffs Exhibit Renovation Project, bringing attention to the redevelopment of the marine wildlife attraction in Brooklyn. Mamdani announced the funding on his social media accounts, thanking those who hosted his visit to the aquarium. Sea Cliffs is an outdoor exhibit housing southern sea otters, sea lions, harbour seals and black-footed penguins. The investment comes against the backdrop of a wider city-funded construction project that has been in planning for years. New York City’s capital strategy lists $23.4 million for Sea Cliffs construction, although the relationship between the two funding figures remains unclear.Zohran Mamdani’s $2 million investment targets Sea Cliffs exhibit upgradesIn a social media post, Mamdani described the $2 million investment as funding for the Sea Cliffs Exhibit Renovation Project at the New York Aquarium. He thanked Council Member Kayla Santosuosso for hosting his visit and added a light-hearted reference to Pickles, a seal associated with the encounter.The post confirms the investment but does not specify the individual upgrades it will fund, the construction schedule or the expected improvements to the animals’ habitats.The New York Aquarium is located in Coney Island, Brooklyn, and is operated by the Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS), which runs wildlife parks and conservation programmes.What is the Sea Cliffs exhibit at New York Aquarium?Sea Cliffs is an outdoor exhibit where visitors can observe marine animals associated with rocky coastal environments. According to the aquarium’s official website, it features southern sea otters, sea lions, harbour seals and black-footed penguins. The habitat gives visitors an opportunity to learn about these species and their environments.Penguins use rocky cliffs for nesting, while sea otters and seals sometimes rest outside the water. The exhibit allows visitors to observe these behaviours while learning about the animals.The aquarium also provides a home for rescued southern sea otters, which are native to the California coast. Its official website lists three current residents. In October 2024, two rescued female southern sea otters made their public debut at the aquarium after being deemed unable to return to the wild. The aquarium has provided a home for 11 rescued sea otters since 1991, according to WCS.Sea Cliffs renovation has a history of delaysThe renovation project has a longer history in New York City’s capital construction records. A project detail document published in April 2023 listed August 2015 as the original start date for developing the project’s scope. The document also identified budgetary constraints as a reason for delays.At the time, the revised project schedule anticipated substantial completion in June 2027, followed by a final punch-list stage and project closure in September 2027. These dates were projections recorded in the 2023 document and should not be treated as confirmation of the project's current construction timeline.New York City’s FY2026-2035 Ten-Year Capital Strategy lists $23.4 million for construction of the Sea Cliffs exhibit. This provides context for the scale of the wider project, but the available documents do not establish whether the newly announced $2 million is additional to that allocation or forms part of an existing funding plan.New York Aquarium’s role in marine conservationThe New York Aquarium is operated by the Wildlife Conservation Society, an organisation involved in wildlife conservation, research and public education. Situated on Coney Island’s waterfront, the aquarium offers visitors opportunities to learn about aquatic species and the ecosystems they inhabit. Its exhibits include Sea Cliffs and Sea Change, which provides underwater views of sea lions, harbour seals, sea otters and penguins.Sea Change also explores climate change and its effects on marine ecosystems and ocean life. It opened on July 1, 2022, as the final public exhibit to reopen following damage caused by Superstorm Sandy in 2012. The aquarium had spent years rebuilding and restoring its facilities after the storm.The Sea Cliffs renovation is part of the aquarium’s wider infrastructure development. articles.title: Could US midterms reshape Pakistan’s relationship with Washington?
articles.summary: Pakistan has gained diplomatic visibility under Trump, but analysts question how much the relationship has delivered.
articles.body:
Islamabad, Pakistan – Addressing a mixed crowd of the diaspora and policy experts in New York late in September, Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar was asked about challenges in New Delhi’s relationship with the United States under President Donald Trump.

“Well, I think if I stand back and look at the relationship … I note that much of the world has had a more difficult relationship with the US,” Jaishankar responded.

Pakistan – perhaps uncomfortably for rival India – is an exception.

Trump’s tumultuous second term has seen him rock the global economy with tariffs and the Iran war, upend decades of trust with traditional US allies, and attempt to shred international law and the institutions that govern it. From Europe to the Middle East to East Asia, allies that counted on a US security umbrella are scrambling to build alternative partnerships, unable to rely on Washington for help if they are attacked. Leaders of nations that have been staunch US supporters have instead found themselves targeted – often personally – by Trump.

Yet amid this churn, Pakistan has managed to turn what was a deeply troubled relationship with the US into a partnership that Trump repeatedly touts, even as the government in Islamabad has faced mounting criticism domestically over allegations that it is crushing political opposition and entrenching military rule in all but name.

As the US holds its midterm elections on November 3, with the power in the House of Representatives and Senate at stake, Pakistan is one country that will prefer success for Trump and his Republican Party, which at present is expected to lose critical seats in both chambers.

“The prime minister of Pakistan – terrific man – said that Donald Trump was responsible for saving 30 million lives and probably many more than that,” the US president said, addressing the United Nations General Assembly in September, referring to Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif – and to a war that appears to have endeared Islamabad to Trump.

After decades of strong ties, US-Pakistan relations had plummeted in recent years , as successive US presidents built close ties with rival India, and Islamabad was seen in Washington as duplicitous over its role in supporting both the US and, at the time, the Afghan Taliban.

As presidents, Trump in his first term and then Joe Biden used harsh words to describe Pakistan.

But two months into his second term, in March 2025, Trump thanked Pakistan in his address to Congress for helping arrest a suspect in the 2021 Abbey Gate bombing at Kabul airport.

Then, in May, came a major turning point. India and Pakistan fought an intense, four-day war after armed fighters killed 26 tourists in Indian-administered Kashmir. The war ended in a ceasefire on May 10. Trump announced it first , and Pakistan thanked him for mediating it, but India rejects his account, insisting that the war was ended through bilateral talks.

Since then, Pakistan’s top leadership has been welcomed at the White House , tariffs on its exports have been cut, and Islamabad has mediated between Washington and Tehran in their ongoing war.

Trump hosted Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, for lunch at the White House – the first time for a Pakistani army chief who is not the country’s president. Trump has described Munir as his “favourite field marshal”.

Pakistan also nominated Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize. On October 9, the day the Nobel Peace Prize was announced for South African jurist Navi Pillay, Sharif posted on X: “President Donald Trump played a historic role in advancing peace in South Asia. His timely intervention helped bring Pakistan and India back from the brink and secure a ceasefire, that is holding till today.”

Analysts say Islamabad’s relevance to Washington extends beyond South Asia.

“Pakistan is now an important player that must be seen within the Middle East security framework,” Qamar Cheema, executive director of the Islamabad-based Sanober Institute, told Al Jazeera.

A trade deal in July 2025 cut US tariffs on Pakistani goods from 29 to 19 percent. Memorandums of understanding with US firms on minerals , cryptocurrency and drones have followed.

Imran Khan, a geopolitical analyst and former Pakistan country director at the United States Institute of Peace, said Islamabad’s closeness to Trump had significantly raised its diplomatic profile.

“But at the same time, you could say that Pakistan has not gained anything directly from the Americans, apart from some intangibles: Its diplomatic profile and its geopolitical relevance,” he told Al Jazeera.

Following the US-Israel attacks on Iran in February, Pakistan brokered a ceasefire between Washington and Tehran on April 8 and hosted the highest-level direct talks between the two sides since 1979.

In June, the US and Iran agreed to the 14-point Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding . “Pakistan was able to bring the United States and Iran under one roof after 47 years,” Cheema said.

But the 60-day period for further talks expired in mid-August without an extension.

Munir returned to Tehran on October 20, his fifth visit since the war began. Iranian officials said they had nothing new to offer Washington. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said threats and military manoeuvres would not influence Iran’s decisions. No breakthrough was announced.

“The Iran war continues to loom large in the Gulf, especially as there are increased indications that the US, possibly again with Israel, will relaunch attacks after their respective elections,” Grace Wermenbol, a former US national security official and senior visiting fellow at the German Marshall Fund, told Al Jazeera. Israel’s elections are scheduled for October 27.

Trump goes into the midterms with historically low popularity numbers. His approval rating stood at 30 percent in a Pew Research Center survey conducted between September 28 and October 4, down from 37 percent in January.

Khan, the analyst, said Democrats would prioritise treaty alliances such as NATO if they won both chambers.

“[In that case], the Senate and the House of Representatives, where the Democrats would have a majority, would lean more towards India than Pakistan,” he said.

Wermenbol, who is also an executive director of the Paris-based advisory firm Boussole Mondiale, said allies and partners were asking whether the midterms could shape US foreign policy in the short term.

In the longer term, she said, the result could foreshadow a change in the White House in 2028 or 2029.

For Pakistan, the question is how to position itself.

Cheema said Pakistan should not shape its approach around whether Trump’s influence grows or weakens. Its strength, he said, lay in its Middle East relevance and role in protecting US interests.

“It is not just a question of Trump’s weakening influence. It is a question of how Pakistan can stay relevant,” he said.

Khan said a weaker Trump might change little in the short term but warned that it could mark the beginning of the end of Pakistan’s current importance.

“But what it does not change is Pakistan’s amplified geopolitical profile globally, and its increasing national security and defence relevance in West Asia,” Khan told Al Jazeera. “That is not going to change whether the Trump administration is strong or weak, or whether Trump is around or not.”

articles.title: Netanyahu's political survival on the line as Israel votes
articles.summary: JERUSALEM, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces a fight for political survival in Israel's election on Tuesday, with voters weighing hi...
articles.body:
Israel holds first general election since October 7 Hamas attack

JERUSALEM, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces a fight for political survival in Israel's election on Tuesday, with voters weighing his leadership after the 2023 Hamas-led attacks, wars in Gaza and with Iran, and Israel's deepening international isolation.

Yet Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving leader with 19 years in ‌office, remains a formidable survivor, with nationalist politics increasingly entrenched and Israel's fragmented system potentially leaving him best placed to form a government.

Opinion polls show a close race between ‌Netanyahu's Likud party and its right-wing allies and a rival alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff and security hawk with backers on the right and in the centre.

Voters began casting ballots after polling stations ​opened at 7 a.m. (0500 GMT). The polls close at 10 p.m. (2000 GMT). Netanyahu has campaigned on his wartime leadership and his alliance with US President Donald Trump, who has endorsed him and joined Israel in waging war on Iran. Netanyahu said on Sunday that Trump was prepared to act again to "finally" remove the Iranian threat, but only if Netanyahu remained in power.

Eisenkot has accused Netanyahu of "relying on a campaign of fear-mongering, lies and threats," and said he was confident Trump would work "in full cooperation with any leader chosen by the people."

Netanyahu may again depend on far-right leaders Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich to ‌form a government. Both have faced sanctions from some Western countries ⁠that accuse them of inciting violence against Palestinians, while Ben-Gvir's Jewish Power party has gained support in opinion polls.

Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a clear path to power. If neither can form a governing coalition in the 120-seat parliament, Netanyahu could stay on as caretaker until another election is held next ⁠year.

The Israeli Central Election Committee said 7.3 million Israelis are eligible to vote, some 330,000 of them for the first time.

The election follows one of Israel's most turbulent periods since its establishment in 1948, shaped by the trauma of the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks, Israel's subsequent military assault in Gaza and deep domestic divisions over the policies of Netanyahu's right-wing government.

For many of Netanyahu's opponents, the election ​turns ​on accountability for the security failures of October 7, Israel's deadliest day.

Mali Hajaj, an Education Ministry employee and ​Eisenkot supporter, said "the most important thing is the establishment of a national ‌inquiry because that's where our healing will come from."

Lisa Tortor said she hoped Netanyahu would go and "they can form a new government and do some of the repairing of the damage that Bibi has done for Jews all over the world and for Israel, and Israel's image." Bibi is Netanyahu's nickname.

But Nof Gabay, an 18-year-old Likud supporter, rejected the idea Netanyahu was to blame for October 7 and called him "the right man for the state of Israel."

"Netanyahu managed the war in the best possible way," Gabay said.

Israel flattened much of Gaza in the offensive launched after October 7, when Hamas-led militants killed 1,200 people and took another 251 hostage. Gaza health authorities say Israeli attacks killed 74,000 people.

Israel also dealt heavy blows to Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon and ‌traded strikes with Iran before a 12-day aerial campaign against Iranian nuclear sites in 2025 and this year's ​joint US-Israeli war.

Eisenkot has said Israel's next government must prevent Iran from acquiring a military nuclear capability, either by ​force or through an "arrangement" such as a US-backed diplomatic solution.

Like nearly all Jewish-led ​parties in Israel, Eisenkot opposes the two-state solution that underpinned decades of peace negotiations with the Palestinians.

But he has criticised Jewish settler violence against Palestinians ‌in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, which has surged since 2023 and strained ​Israel's ties with Western states, and opposes Netanyahu's far-right ​coalition partners Ben-Gvir and Smotrich.

In some bastions of Likud support, disenchanted voters have been going door to door to turn voters against Netanyahu. Some have turned away from Netanyahu as he battles corruption charges he denies in a long-running criminal trial.

A high turnout among voters from Israel's Arab minority, Israeli by citizenship but Palestinian by heritage, could help ​nudge Israel's complex coalition arithmetic in favour of Eisenkot.

Though Eisenkot has ruled ‌out partnering with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values, analysts see a scenario where they prop up a minority government he leads in order to ​ensure Netanyahu is removed from office.

"My expectation is that we will have only a slight majority either way. No landslide," said Israeli political analyst Amotz Asa-El of ​the Shalom Hartman Institute.

(Additional reporting by Maayan Lubell; Writing by Tom Perry; Editing by Howard Goller)

articles.title: Australia: Sunscreen brands face stricter rules after safety scandal
articles.summary: The reforms come after a report found some popular sunscreens were far less effective than advertised.
articles.body:
Australian sunscreen manufacturers will be subject to stricter rules in the wake of a safety scandal that saw popular brands pulled off shelves.

The reforms, announced by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) on Tuesday, include stronger testing and quality requirements for specific ingredients.

This comes after a bombshell report last year by consumer advocacy group Choice which found that some popular sunscreens did not provide the level of protection their manufacturers claimed.

The new proposed regulations are "about making SPF claims more reliable" and giving the agency "faster access to evidence when concerns arise", Robyn Langham, the TGA's chief medical adviser, tells the BBC.

"Australians expect the SPF on the label to be backed by robust evidence," she said in a statement over email.

"These proposed reforms put that expectation at the centre of sunscreen regulation, with stronger testing requirements for the finished product consumers buy and repeat testing throughout its time on the market."

Under the new regulations proposed by the TGA, cosmetic sunscreen brands will also be limited in the skin protection factor (SPF) claims they can make.

This is to ensure "clear distinction for consumers" between sunscreens that are mainly made for UV protection and cosmetic products where UV protection is a secondary function.

Suppliers would also be required to provide their SPF testing data to the TGA when they list a sunscreen , and keep periodically testing the product throughout its shelf life.

Under current regulations, it's not mandatory for sunscreen manufacturers to provide testing data to the TGA unless requested.

The TGA said the reforms would be "implemented in stages, with further consultation where required".

The Choice report, published in June 2025, found that 16 of 20 tested sunscreens - including several premium, expensive brands - failed to live up to their advertised SPF rating.

The sunscreen scandal shocking Australia - the world's skin cancer hotspot

Australia sunscreen scandal grows as more products pulled off shelves

One product, Ultra Violette's Lean Screen Skinscreen, which was voluntarily recalled last year, was marketed as having an SPF of 50+ but was found to offer only SPF 4.

The scandal sparked massive backlash in Australia, which has the highest rate of skin cancer in the world.

More than a dozen products were pulled from shelves or had their sales suspended as a result of the scandal.

The TGA proposed sweeping reforms to the sunscreen industry earlier this year , which included plans to make sunscreen labelling simpler and more oversight at testing labs.

Its statement on Tuesday said that changes to labelling would be made after further review and consultation.

Choice welcomed the reforms, saying in a statement on Tuesday that it was "pleased to see" the stricter rules proposed by the TGA.

However, the group pointed out that the TGA has not proposed to "routinely monitor and evaluate test results".

Choice also argued that that sunscreen test results should not be provided only to the TGA - as proposed by the regulator - but rather made publicly available and routinely monitored, "in the interest of transparency and public safety".

Additional reporting by Tiffanie Turnbull

articles.title: Palestinian citizens of Israel can vote, but cannot expect change
articles.summary: Elections cannot stop the accelerated process of ‘recolonisation’ of 1948 Palestinian communities.
articles.body:
For the majority of Israelis, the general election on October 27 is a choice between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the forces that oppose him, led by former general Gadi Eisenkot. But for the Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up 20 percent of the population, the upcoming polls present a different dilemma.

As the political mainstream in Israel continues to shift to the far right, Palestinian citizens face growing threats to their political and collective rights. Palestinian communities in Israel experience increased violence, while settlers are encroaching on their boundaries. The recent push to expand policing and militarisation of civilian life is another source of growing anxiety within the Palestinian population.

In this context, the anti-Netanyahu bloc does not seem to offer the prospect of policy reversal or change. Therefore, the question on many Palestinian minds is whether voting in the Israeli elections can make any difference at all.

Since the Nakba of 1948, the Palestinians who managed to remain in their homes in what was declared as territory of the new State of Israel have had a different fate than the Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza. In 1952, they were granted Israeli citizenship, and in 1966, the martial law under which they were forced to live was lifted.

Although Palestinian citizens of Israel have the right to vote and participate in politics, citizenship has not shielded them from the broader system of dispossession and attempts to reshape their Palestinian identity and national belonging.

Through land confiscation and the regulation of education and culture, the Israeli state has sought to detach Palestinians from their historical roots and collective past, promoting instead a model of the “Arab Israeli” as a citizen whose identity is separate from its Palestinian and Arab national context.

Formal citizenship has not secured substantive equality for Palestinians as they face discriminatory laws, systemic underfunding of basic services, and political and socioeconomic marginalisation.

Instead of engaging in direct violence towards Palestinian citizens – as it has done in the West Bank and Gaza – the Israeli state has instead “outsourced” brutality to criminal networks.

As a result, Palestinian communities have faced killings, shootings, bombings and arson while Israeli law enforcement has largely ignored the problem. More recently, this problem has escalated, as organised crime groups obtained advanced weapons reportedly stolen from Israeli army stockpiles or smuggled across borders. This growing militarisation of organised crime has claimed hundreds of lives.

In parallel, Israeli settlements next to Palestinian communities have expanded, accompanied by accelerated seizure of land. This process of “recolonisation” began in mixed cities, such as Jaffa and Lydd, where religious-nationalist settler groups started establishing themselves in Palestinian neighbourhoods in 2021.

Since October 2023, this process has accelerated. In August, Israel’s Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich unveiled his party’s plan to “Judaise” the Naqab and northern Israel. He proposes to add one million Jewish residents to the two regions, establishing 40 new settlements and dozens of farms, expanding existing settlements, and creating hundreds of thousands of new housing units.

The idea is to extend the model of territorial control from the occupied West Bank into the Naqab and northern Israel, where Palestinian communities are concentrated.

There are also indications that the policing of Palestinian towns and villages could increasingly fall under the National Guard, established under National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.

The idea of creating the force was prompted by the May 2021 protests, known as the Dignity Uprising, which spread across Palestinian communities in Lydd, Haifa, Umm al-Fahm, and dozens of other towns and villages.

Ben-Gvir has advocated expanding the state’s capacity to suppress such unrest. Although the National Guard’s precise role and operational framework remain under development, its potential deployment against mass protests raises serious concerns about the right to protest and the protection of democratic freedoms.

The government has strengthened settler security squads and integrated them into a broader security framework, raising concerns about the growing role of armed civilian groups in enforcing control over Palestinian communities.

At the same time, Ben-Gvir has widened access to personal firearms, issuing 300,000 gun licences since taking office.

Together, these measures normalise civilian policing and deepen the militarisation of everyday life, reinforcing the unequal distribution of coercive power in a society structured on the dispossession and subordination of Palestinians.

Parties seeking to represent Palestinian citizens of Israel, such as the United Arab List (Ra’am), led by Mansour Abbas, have long argued that parliamentary participation and support for the anti-Netanyahu camp can help remove the far right from power and halt its settler-colonial agenda. But the party’s own track record proves this premise wrong.

Ra’am joined the coalition government formed after the elections in 2021, which excluded Netanyahu, but it failed to bring about fundamental changes in the conditions of Palestinian citizens. The coalition was fragile and often rocked by deep ideological contradictions.

In 2022, Mazen Ghnaim, a member of Ra’am, publicly acknowledged that he could not push through policies that would benefit the Palestinian population, despite his party being part of the ruling coalition and despite promises being made that such policies would be accepted. He also lamented the heavy criticism he faced whenever he was visiting Palestinian communities.

Ra’am’s experience in that coalition illustrated the challenge of sustaining Palestinian political participation in a government whose other constituent parties uphold exclusionary nationalist policies.

The problem, therefore, extends beyond Netanyahu himself: Palestinian support for the anti-Netanyahu camp cannot translate into meaningful policies that challenge the broader structures of discrimination and dispossession Palestinian citizens of Israel face.

Voting may offer a way to slow down this project, but it cannot reverse the deeper transformation taking place within Israeli society. The cultural shift towards fascism extends beyond the government and its political leadership, becoming increasingly embedded in social attitudes and everyday life.

That said, I believe another four years of far-right rule would pose an immediate threat to Palestinian communities and their rights. Therefore, I will vote in Tuesday’s election.

But Palestinians need to recognise that electoral participation must be accompanied by a more radical political response capable of confronting the structures and ideologies driving this transformation. This requires, among other things, reforming the High Follow-Up Committee for Arab Citizens of Israel and rooting it more firmly in Palestinian society through popular committees and grassroots organising.

It also demands a broader commitment to democratisation and de-Zionisation across historic Palestine, as part of a larger political project aimed at building a different future through alternative institutions, mechanisms, and forms of collective action.

Whatever the Israeli state might claim, the fate of the Palestinian citizens of Israel is tied to the fate of the rest of the Palestinian population. That is a realisation that Palestinian political leaders must finally embrace.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: 1 in 4 South Asian Americans who backed Trump in 2024 now plan to vote Democrat in midterms: Survey
articles.summary: At least 25% of South Asian Americans who voted for US President Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election plan to back Democratic candidates in the
articles.body: At least 25% of South Asian Americans who voted for US President Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election plan to back Democratic candidates in the November 3 midterm elections, according to a survey by advocacy group Indian American Impact.The survey identified the cost of living (65%), healthcare (53%), jobs and wages (33%), and education (28%) as the key issues influencing voters ahead of the midterms.Of the 800 registered South Asian voters surveyed, 87% were Indian-Americans, while the remaining 13% were from Pakistani, Bangladeshi, Sri Lankan, Nepali, Bhutanese, Maldivian, Afghani, Khmer and Burmese communities.Among respondents who voted for Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election, 96% said they planned to vote for a Democratic candidate in the upcoming polls.The survey found that while 67% of South Asian Americans who voted for Trump continued to support Republicans, 25% planned to vote for Democrats.The findings come as early voting has begun in several states, including Texas, where Democratic nominee James Talarico is locked in a tight race against Republican Ken Paxton, who has Trump's backing.Vasant Bhatt, a 21-year-old second-generation Indian-American who interned on Senator Ted Cruz's election campaign in 2024, said in a social media post that he had voted for Talarico."I just cast my ballot for James Talarico. As a second-generation Indian American, I am thoroughly disgusted by the xenophobia, racial resentment, and increasingly brazen attacks on my identity," Bhatt wrote.The survey also pointed to widespread concerns about discrimination. As many as 90% of registered voters said they had experienced discrimination or knew someone who had, while 48% said they had personally faced it.“It comes as no surprise that a quarter of Trump’s 2024 voters in our community plan to vote Democratic. This community can make the margin, and we are working to reach every voter who can,” Chintan Patel, executive director of Indian American Impact, said in a statement.The survey found that 16% of respondents had not voted in any general election since 2020.It also highlighted a broader sense of disillusionment with elected representatives. While 78% of respondents believed their vote could bring about change, 79% felt elected officials quickly lost touch with ordinary people. Another 67% said public officials did not care about the views of people like them, while 43% felt they had no say in government decisions.The findings underscore the potential electoral influence of South Asian American voters, particularly in closely contested states.Michigan has around 187,000 South Asian residents. Nearly 30,000 registered South Asian voters did not vote in 2022, exceeding the roughly 19,000-vote margin that decided the state's 2024 Senate race.Texas, meanwhile, has more than 700,000 South Asian residents, with nearly 100,000 registered South Asian voters having sat out the 2022 elections.The Indian-American community also has a significant presence in California, Texas, New Jersey, New York, Washington, Illinois, Pennsylvania and Georgia.In battleground states such as Georgia, Pennsylvania, Michigan and North Carolina, where electoral contests can be decided by narrow margins, even a shift of one or two percentage points in voter support could influence the outcome.You use AI every day. articles.title: Budget 2026: Will Andy Burnham's Makerfield test be met?
articles.summary: People in the prime minister's constituency say rising costs are squeezing household finances.
articles.body:
On a wet Tuesday in October, Platt Bridge Community Centre, near Wigan, is alive with the music of Shania Twain. About 30 women and one man are line dancing to her hit Man! I Feel Like a Woman! The class is so popular that the centre has recently introduced an extra session to meet demand.

The community centre is in the heart of Andy Burnham's constituency, Makerfield, and they know all about budgeting here. It is run entirely by volunteers and has recently had to raise thousands of pounds for a new roof.

Norman Smith is one of the trustees. He says running the centre comes with tremendous financial challenges.

"It's a very old building, and sometimes the trustees feel like they're trying to keep all the plates spinning, it's very hard at times."

As well as line dancing, the centre is home to Wigan table tennis club. It also offers a food bank and a warm space.

Smith says the centre is an essential part of the Platt Bridge community.

"No one gets paid for working here. We have around 500 people using the centre. Financially it couldn't run without the volunteers."

Platt Bridge is one of the most deprived parts of Wigan.

When Andy Burnham won the Makerfield by-election, he said the constituency would not be a "stepping stone" to No 10 , although he went on to become prime minister.

Instead, he said he wanted it to be a "touchstone", with every government policy or announcement having to meet a "Makerfield test". If it works there, it will work for other communities like it.

In his victory speech in June, Burnham said: "A Makerfield test at the heart of British politics will make sure that the places Westminster has neglected will now get fairness."

John Healey's first Budget will be a real test of that.

Will people in Ashton feel they have more or less money when they do their weekly shop? Will a small business in Abram have more confidence to expand and take on more staff?

Zoe Billingham, from the think tank IPPR North, says the Budget will be a "balancing act" between the pressures people are facing from the rising cost of living and the economic headwinds caused by events such as the war in Iran.

She says it will be a "really important budget to show who they [the government] stand for".

She wants to know who will be asked to shoulder those economic pressures and who will receive support?

"The Makerfield test is a really valuable way of making sure that the economy works in service of ordinary people," she says.

Back at the community centre, Sue Hughes, chair of the trustees, thinks the government is already recognising the area's needs.

Platt Bridge and nearby Spring View have been awarded £20m over the next 10 years through Pride in Place funding.

"I can't complain about the support this area is being given, but more support is always welcome," she says.

"Platt Bridge is a really vibrant community, despite being so deprived. So the community itself deserves that support."

Burnham's government has made several announcements aimed at tackling the cost of living, including a £2 bus fare cap , removing VAT on domestic electricity bills and business rates relief for pubs and live music venues .

But the prime minister recently admitted it was not enough and hinted that there could be further support in the Budget.

Sophie Lowe, 29, from Abram, has a two-year-old daughter. She says she has not yet felt the benefit of any of Burnham's policies.

"I found it hard going back to work, but we needed the two incomes just to cover the bills."

She says she had to leave her job in Merseyside and find one closer to home because the cost of petrol was too high.

The price at the pumps is also an issue for one of the line dancers, Joanne Ainscow, who says she now spends at least £20 more every time she fills up.

But the 57-year-old foster carer also thinks the government can do more to help workers like her by exempting them from council tax.

Some local authorities offer a 100% discount or full exemption for foster carers in the UK, while many others do not.

"We are all doing the same job, so it should be the same across the board. It should be equal," she says.

Nicha Rowson, 35, says she believes the Platt Bridge community is "being heard" under Burnham's stewardship.

She says that when residents speak to their local MP and councillors, they are "taking in our voices".

She believes that if politicians listen to what residents are saying, Makerfield could become "this amazing place".

Taking a rest from line dancing, Karen Jones, 67, from Ashton-in-Makerfield, says she will be watching the Budget on Wednesday with interest.

"I want to see what they can do for people," she says.

She wants the chancellor to look at helping people keep more of their money.

"People are struggling to earn a decent living and then they're taxed quite a lot on it, there should be a little bit more relief for them, I think."

The Budget coincides with Andy Burnham's first 100 days in office.

The steps he and the chancellor take on Wednesday could determine how well the next 100 days are received.

articles.title: Rare zebra-striped bee in West a 'huge surprise'
articles.summary: A zebra-striped bee is seen in Somerset for the first time, offering hope in restored saltmarshes.
articles.body:
A tiny zebra-striped bee, usually found along England's south and east coasts, has made an unexpected journey to the West Country.

The rare sea aster mining bee has been spotted at Steart Marshes in Somerset by naturalist Nigel Phillips, who said the find "was a huge surprise".

The Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust said saltmarsh restoration work at the nature reserve had helped create the perfect home for the newcomer.

The charity says the discovery shows how rare species and wildlife can thrive by restoring coastal habitats.

We're just tax-collectors, say pub landlords asking for help

Tributes paid to couple killed in A358 crash

Work on controversial £2.35m cycle path paused

The sea aster mining bee has a particular taste in flowers and relies on the sea aster, a pink and yellow flower that blooms on coastal marshes, as summer moves into autumn.

The restoration project at Steart Marshes was completed in 2014, transforming former farmland into a coastal wetland by allowing seawater to flow back across the fields.

The reserve supports a wide variety of coastal wildflowers, including plenty of sea aster, which is thought to have finally attracted the bees to the Steart peninsula.

"There were lots of them and several colonial nest areas in the dry sandy ground," said Phillips.

"At the time I thought they were only found in salt marsh areas around the Thames estuary."

Of the 290 invertebrate species found in these habitats across the UK, 148 can only be found in saltmarshes.

Site manager Bay Alys Laver said: "People usually associate saltmarshes with huge flocks of wading birds, geese and ducks, but there is so much life here that goes unnoticed.

"Spotting such a rare species here is a testament to the brilliant work our staff do in maintaining the reserve in concert with local graziers.

"I was so happy to hear that we have been found by our first sea aster mining bees."

articles.title: Palestine weekly: West Bank under siege as Israelis go to the polls
articles.summary: Israel sealed the West Bank, emptied parts of Hebron and tightened the squeeze on Gaza as its election campaign closed.
articles.body:
While Israelis go to the polls this week in one of the most consequential elections in years, many Palestinians in the West Bank have been confined to their homes or neighbourhoods as a wave of Israeli military operations around Hebron continues.

The West Bank city has been in a state of lockdown since two Palestinian gunmen opened fire at an army checkpoint at Hebron’s northern entrance on Friday, killing two Israeli soldiers and wounding three. After the suspects were killed, Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered the isolation of Hebron and said troops would go house to house in the gunmen’s neighbourhood. “We will act to destroy this place, to change it completely,” he proclaimed.

What followed has been a mass displacement operation in the Hebron area, echoing last year’s military expulsions of three refugee camps, alongside widespread destruction in the neighbourhoods targeted by the army, evoking scenes out of Gaza.

During the weekend, soldiers ordered residents of al-Jalda and Ein Deir Baha neighbourhoods out by loudspeaker, according to residents. Thousands have been forced out of their homes already, with Defence Minister Israel Katz saying people would not be allowed back “until we’ve finished dealing with all the Hamas issues in Hebron”. By Monday, the governorate’s fourth day under closure, at least 3,171 Palestinians from 488 families had been forced out, according to Hebron Municipality data cited by the Wafa news agency. Hebron Governor Khaled Dudin said Israeli forces had searched more than 500 homes, arrested more than 70 people and fragmented the city with 128 closed gates and 120 checkpoints.

The Palestinian Prisoner’s Society says the displaced include 127 infants, 81 pregnant women and 26 people with disabilities, and that at least 47 people have been detained in Hebron since Friday .

Bulldozers razed a three-apartment building belonging to Riyad Amrish, as well as a tile and ceramics factory, an auto-parts shop and other businesses in Farsh al-Hawa. Israel’s Channel 12 said Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich ordered the demolitions.

Israeli NGO B’Tselem warned the operation amounts to “collective punishment and acts that could constitute war crimes”.

But Hebron is only the most prominent of multiple sieges happening at different scales, with years-long efforts to strategically encircle Palestinian communities in the West Bank now being employed to devastating effect:

Homes: The three-week siege by Israeli settlers of the family of Yusuf Shanaran in Wadi al-Rakheem, Masafer Yatta continues, with the family unable to leave or receive aid for days at a time without army coordination, Shanaran told Al Jazeera on Monday. In Umm Safa, northwest of Ramallah, village Mayor Marwan Sabah said Mohammad al-Obaiyat’s 1954 house received a demolition order with a November 11 deadline after months with a gate blocking its road. Settlers have since been filmed attempting to break into the family home, which has been besieged for nearly a month, with few supplies entering during that time.

A village: Madama, south of Nablus, is only just emerging from a two-week siege of its four entrances, with heavy restrictions remaining at its just-opened northern entrance, according to villagers. A kindergarten principal there told Al Jazeera she lifts children over the barrier one by one .

A region: Twelve Masafer Yatta communities in the southern West Bank were cut off for several days, with about 50 teachers unable to reach their schools, and Wafa reported that Bethlehem governorate’s roads were closed for several days.

A territory: The Israeli army barred Palestinian workers from illegal Israeli settlements on Sunday and Monday and will close all crossings on election day .

The only Palestinians who can vote – Palestinian citizens of Israel – may face issues at the polls, too; Israel’s Channel 12 reported that Netanyahu’s Likud party was preparing to challenge results from Arab polling stations before a vote had been cast.

This year’s olive harvest has drawn unprecedented levels of settler pogroms, theft and closed-military-zone orders. The Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission has counted 482 attacks on the harvest by Sunday across nine governorates, Wafa reported.

At the same time, Israel released nine of 10 settlers arrested following last week’s attacks on a foreign journalist and diplomats. The attacks have continued undeterred. Wafa reported 17 attacks on farmers and their property on Thursday, and the commission documented 21 in 12 hours on Friday. The past week’s harvest-related incidents fall into a handful of repeating patterns:

Theft of olives and equipment in at least a dozen villages, including Sinjil, Silwad, Berin, Beit Iksa, al-Lubban Asharqiya, Kafr Malek, Ein Arik and Deir Ballut, according to Wafa and local reports. Near Immatin, at least 25 masked settlers sent three tractors and two trailers rolling down a hillside, destroying the equipment and olives on board.

Assaults in at least 15 places, among them Burin, where stones left three farmers with head wounds; Ein Arik, where The Times of Israel reported a farmer suffered fractures; and Beit Iksa, al-Lubban Asharqiya and Kafr Malek, where pickers were pepper-sprayed. Settlers fired live rounds at pickers in Berin and Osarin, and smashed cars and trucks in Marda, Wad Qaddoum and Sinjil, Wafa and local monitors reported.

Detentions and expulsions in at least a dozen places. Fifteen farmers were detained in as-Sawiya on Sunday. In Beit Iksa, where the harvest had been coordinated with the Israeli Civil Administration, Mohammed al-Kiswani was pepper-sprayed and detained; settlers told farmers they would never harvest “with or without coordination”. Land at Deir Jarir and Turmus Aya was declared a closed military zone without orders shown, Ayed Jafry reported – and far-right influencers were brought to film the expulsions for campaign content.

Damage to olive trees in at least 10 locations. Settlers burned dozens of trees in Burqa on Friday, keeping Palestinian Civil Defence crews out, according to Wafa; trees were set on fire in Immatin, Salem and Beit Furik; and a bulldozer uprooted hundreds in Madama, according to villagers. Soldiers uprooted dozens more in Deir Qaddis for a settler road and posted a notice at al-Mughayyir ordering hundreds of trees uprooted and in Khirbet Abu Falah for a “security buffer zone”, giving residents 24 hours to object, Jafry reported.

Arson. In Burqa, settlers set fire on Tuesday to a memorial to Palestinian residents killed and, an hour later, to the home of Jamal Bajes, a Palestinian-American – the second arson at his house in recent months, according to local reports. Local activist networks reported a home was burned in Deir Abu Mishal, and Wafa said settlers tried to set another ablaze in Burin under army protection.

Those joining the harvests in solidarity were targeted, too. United States Democratic congressional candidate Brad Lander was among about 80 volunteers detained near Nahalin on Wednesday and released with a “warning”; Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs accused him of “harvesting headlines”.

Gaza: Managed scarcity as killings continue

The last week in Gaza saw at least 37 more Palestinians killed as Israel’s daily attacks continued. Monday’s daily report from the Gaza Ministry of Health alone recorded 11 deaths – eight newly killed, three recovered from rubble – and 35 wounded, taking the toll since the October 2025 “ceasefire” to 1,559 killed and 5,608 wounded, with a cumulative toll of 74,555.

Majdi Mohammad Fakhri Hassan, a child, shot near the Happy City resort south of Khan Younis; Rafif Raed Lubad, 17, shot in the head in Jabalia; and Fatima Abu Laban, killed in Tal al-Dhahab, northwest of Beit Lahiya on Saturday, according to Wafa.

Three security guards – Sami Baroud, Ashraf Dahlan and Shadi Abu Ataya – at the Islamic University in Gaza City on Sunday, after an earlier strike wounded seven students. Israel said it was targeting a Hamas operative.

For days, hunger worsened with crossings into Gaza shut: Flour stocks ran out, leaving seven of 20 commercial bakeries open, Abdul Nasser al-Ajrami of the bakers’ association told Wafa, and a tray of eggs reached a price of 60 shekels ($19.50).

The pressure began to ease somewhat on the evening of October 23, as Israel told traders that commercial goods would resume and an Egyptian committee delivered flour, Mohammad Abu Warda of the private sector’s emergency committee said.

articles.title: Jon Bon Jovi's Toms River restaurant welcomes diners who cannot afford a meal; in the first half of 2026, more than 80% of the meals it served went to guests experiencing food insecurity
articles.summary: More than 80% of the meals served at Jon Bon Jovi's JBJ Soul Kitchen restaurant in Toms River, New Jersey, went to guests experiencing food insecurity
articles.body: More than 80% of the meals served at Jon Bon Jovi's JBJ Soul Kitchen restaurant in Toms River, New Jersey, went to guests experiencing food insecurity during the first half of 2026, according to the Jon Bon Jovi Soul Foundation. The foundation's announcement, published on its official website as part of a sponsorship appeal for the restaurant's annual Chilli Cook-Off, highlights the role of its community restaurant in providing nutritious meals to people who cannot afford them.Unlike conventional restaurants, JBJ Soul Kitchen does not list fixed prices on its menu. Instead, diners who can afford their meals are encouraged to make a suggested donation and contribute towards the cost of feeding someone else. Guests unable to pay are welcomed to enjoy a meal and learn about volunteering opportunities, according to the restaurant's official website. The approach is designed to address hunger while allowing people to dine in a setting that promotes dignity and community rather than treating food assistance as a separate service.How the pay-it-forward model worksJBJ Soul Kitchen is a nonprofit community restaurant established by the Jon Bon Jovi Soul Foundation, which was founded in 2006 to help break the cycle of hunger, poverty and homelessness. The restaurant's model brings together paying customers, volunteers and people experiencing financial hardship around a shared dining experience.Guests who can afford to pay are encouraged to make a suggested donation and cover the cost of another person's meal. Those unable to contribute financially can volunteer their time, with restaurant staff helping them explore opportunities to participate in the community. The arrangement is not a conventional pay-what-you-want system, according to the organisation, but a structured effort to connect meals with volunteering and community support.The restaurant serves a chef-prepared three-course meal, typically including soup or salad, a choice of entree and dessert or fruit. Menus change every two weeks, and ingredients are sourced locally where possible. The restaurant says it aims to ensure that nutritious food is accessible without making the ability to pay a condition for being welcomed at the table.Food assistance alongside other community servicesThe restaurant's work extends beyond providing meals. It collaborates with local organisations to connect guests with resources related to housing, mental health, substance-use support, employment and other essential needs.In a May 22, 2026, feature, the James Beard Foundation described how the restaurant uses food as an entry point for building relationships with people facing difficulties that may not be immediately visible. Founder and programme director Dorothea Bongiovi explained that creating a safe and welcoming environment can help guests feel comfortable discussing their circumstances and seeking assistance.The foundation's feature reported that 78% of diners across the restaurant's operations identified as being in need. It also described how community coordinators work with partner organisations in Monmouth and Ocean counties to connect guests with relevant services. These can include housing assistance, job training, addiction treatment, mental health support and help accessing public benefits.The 78% figure refers to diners identifying as being in need across the restaurant's operations, while the foundation's separate first-half-of-2026 statement specifically reports that more than 80% of meals at the Toms River location went to guests experiencing food insecurity.Toms River's temporary pop-up served more than 15,870 mealsThe restaurant's impact in Ocean County was also evident at a temporary JBJ Soul Kitchen pop-up inside the Ocean County Library in downtown Toms River. Launched in February 2025 at the library's invitation, the initiative aimed to respond to the growing needs of people experiencing homelessness and expand access to meals and community support during the winter Code Blue season.The pop-up closed on April 30, 2026. Before closing, it had served more than 15,870 meals over the previous year, with 79% going to guests in need, according to JBJ Soul Kitchen. More than 1,000 volunteers contributed nearly 4,000 hours of service during the initiative.The programme also connected guests with support beyond food. According to the organisation, it distributed more than 1,350 hygiene kits and made 276 referrals to service providers. These efforts resulted in 13 successful housing placements and nine people securing employment. The figures were also reported by News 12 New Jersey in April 2026.Although the library pop-up has closed, the organisation confirmed that its permanent Toms River restaurant on Hooper Avenue would continue operating. The temporary site's results demonstrate how the same pay-it-forward approach can be extended to meet needs in a specific community, particularly when food insecurity overlaps with homelessness and limited access to essential services.JBJ Soul Kitchen's approach aims to make food assistance part of an ordinary restaurant experience. Rather than separating people who need help from those who can pay, the model encourages them to share the same space and meal.The Jon Bon Jovi Soul Foundation received the 2026 James Beard Foundation Impact Award, recognising its work addressing hunger, poverty and homelessness. articles.title: Sixty Christians killed in Ethiopia’s Oromia region
articles.summary: Church officials say more than 20 people have been injured, while 20 homes have burned down as religious tensions flare.
articles.body:
At least 60 Orthodox Christians were killed in separate attacks on October 20 and 24 in Ethiopia’s Oromia region, church officials reported.

The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church’s holy synod on Monday described the killings as “extremely tragic cruelty and suffering inflicted on our citizens”. More than 20 people were seriously injured and 20 homes burned down in the attacks, it added.

The church said 14 people were killed on October 20 in Gora Silingo, Angada Kebele in Merti district, while another 46 were killed on October 24 in the villages of Tereta, Chole and Birbo in Shirka district. Both districts are located in the Arsi Zone in central Ethiopia’s Oromia region.

The holy synod condemned the killings, saying the attacks violated constitutional protections for life and religious freedom, and threatened Ethiopia’s tradition of peaceful coexistence among different faiths.

It called on government institutions to publicly condemn the attacks, strengthen civilian protection and ensure those responsible are brought to justice.

The church also urged security agencies to provide additional protection to affected communities and take preventive measures against further violence.

The Oromia regional government has pledged to pursue those responsible for the killings.

There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attacks.

According to media reports, a local official accused a newly formed rebel alliance that includes the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) of carrying out the attacks. The OLA has previously denied allegations of attacking civilians.

The killings come amid continuing insecurity in Oromia, Ethiopia’s largest regional state and home to some 40 million, where government forces have been battling armed groups for years.

In July, the Ethiopian Human Rights Council reported that at least 432 civilians and four local militia members had been killed in targeted attacks across East Arsi between 2021-22 and June 1 this year.

The holy synod said it would seek discussions with senior government officials to address the security crisis.

It also announced prayers for the victims on Monday and directed Orthodox churches and monasteries worldwide to hold similar services on Tuesday, following the Divine Liturgy.

The church expressed condolences to the bereaved families and called for urgent measures to ensure that its followers could live and worship without fear.

articles.title: Israel election live updates: Netanyahu battles to stay in power as voters head to the polls
articles.summary: Follow live as Israelis vote in Netanyahu’s first general election since the Hamas-led October 7 attacks and the launch of his controversial war in Gaza.
articles.body:
What to know Israelis head to the polls today for the first nationwide election since the Hamas-led attacks of Oct. 7, 2023, the deadliest day in the country’s history. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is facing one of the most significant electoral tests of his decades-long political career after three years of war, crisis and global outcry over the country's military campaign in the Gaza Strip. Ahead of the vote, Netanyahu’s Likud party was neck and neck with the Israeli military's former Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, who has emerged as his strongest rival in a fraught campaign that has centered on the country's security and future. No single party has ever earned a majority in the Knesset, or parliament, in Israel’s history so it is unlikely we'll know a winner when polls close this evening. Negotiations to build a governing coalition will likely need to take place. Netanyahu has staunchly defended his conduct and the war in Gaza, which has left about 74,500 people dead since Oct. 7, and goes into the election facing an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court. He vehemently rejects a U.N. commission's allegations of perpetrating a genocide in Gaza.

articles.title: Feds crack down on stolen car pipeline to Mexican cartels as 13 charged in border scheme
articles.summary: Operation Southbound Takedown recovered 29 stolen cars worth $1.14 million allegedly funneled through El Paso to Mexican cartels for daily operations.
articles.body: A cross-border pipeline of stolen vehicles allegedly supplied Mexican cartels with cars and trucks to support their criminal operations, federal authorities say, with 13 people now facing charges in the scheme. The vehicles were stolen from private owners and major rental car companies before being driven through El Paso, Texas, and across the border into Mexico, where they were allegedly used to support the cartels’ daily operations, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Texas. Authorities have recovered 29 vehicles worth an estimated $1.14 million as part of the investigation, dubbed Operation Southbound Takedown, prosecutors said. PIRRO WARNS CAR THEFT RING USED NEW TECH TO QUICKLY ACCESS VEHICLES: 'GONE IN 60 SECONDS' Ryan G. McRae, special agent in charge of Homeland Security Investigations in El Paso, said the stolen vehicles reveal a pattern of criminal activity extending beyond auto theft. "These are not isolated property crimes," McRae said. "The stolen vehicles related to Operation Southbound Takedown demonstrate an alarming pattern and are used to support the day-to-day operations of dangerous criminal organizations." Photos released by prosecutors showed a damaged white SUV recovered in Mexico, as well as an armored black SUV and an armored pickup truck. Federal agents and prosecutors began investigating in the spring after identifying a pattern of stolen vehicles being transported to individuals allegedly connected to criminal organizations in Mexico, the U.S. attorney’s office said. NEVADA MAN FUNNELED 140 GUNS TO VIOLENT MEXICAN DRUG CARTELS, INCLUDING POWERFUL 'MILITARY-STYLE' RIFLES: DOJ U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons warned people considering transporting stolen vehicles into Mexico that cartels are exploiting individuals looking to make a "quick buck" to further their criminal operations. Those operations, he said, include "human smuggling, extortion, drug trafficking, and even murder." TRUMP ADMIN'S LIST OF US-DESIGNATED 'FOREIGN TERRORIST' GROUPS IN LATIN AMERICA EXPANDS TO 21 "You are now on notice," Simmons said. "If you provide support to these cartels, many of which have been designated as foreign terrorist organizations, by transporting stolen vehicles out of this country and into Mexico, we will find you, and we will prosecute to the fullest extent of the law." Of the 13 people charged, 11 are U.S. citizens and two are Mexican citizens, prosecutors said. One of the Mexican citizens has a lawful permanent resident card, while the other has a border crossing card. Two of the Americans, Kimberly Aguilar and Marty Gerardo Jr., are in state custody. The other 11 people were federally indicted and arrested between July 22 and Oct. 19, according to prosecutors. All 13 are charged with interstate transportation of stolen property and face up to 10 years in federal prison if convicted. The charges are allegations, and each person is presumed innocent unless proven guilty. The investigation involved Homeland Security Investigations, the FBI and other federal, state and local agencies working through the Homeland Security Task Force. McRae said authorities worked with private-sector partners to disrupt the alleged vehicle theft and transportation network as part of an investigation spanning the United States and Mexico. articles.title: Lucknow airport welcomes its largest-ever commercial aircraft as Saudia’s Boeing 777 makes historic landing with 430 passengers on board
articles.summary: LUCKNOW: In a significant milestone for the city's aviation sector, Chaudhary Charan Singh International Airport witnessed its first commercial airline
articles.body: LUCKNOW: In a significant milestone for the city's aviation sector, Chaudhary Charan Singh International Airport witnessed its first commercial airline operation involving a Boeing 777 (B777) wide-body aircraft on Tuesday, when Saudia Airlines operated its flight with hundreds of passengers.According to official source, Saudia Airlines flight SV-892 landed at Lucknow airport at 3.42am on October 27 with approximately 430 passengers booked.The aircraft subsequently departed as flight SV-893 at 5.39am with around 300 passengers booked.The operation marked a significant development for Lucknow airport, which has traditionally handled commercial flights operated by narrow-body aircraft such as the Airbus A320 and Boeing 737.The Boeing 777 is a long-range, twin-engine wide-body aircraft designed to accommodate substantially more passengers than conventional narrow-body aircraft.
